name: The Sun: Our Star
teaser: The Sun is so massive it holds about 99.8 percent of the solar system's matter, and it's a surprisingly ordinary star — a middle-aged yellow dwarf. Every second it fuses roughly 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium, converting mass into pure energy. The light hitting your face left the Sun eight minutes ago, and without it, Earth would be a frozen ball of rock. One day, five billion years from now, it will swell into a red giant and swallow the inner planets. Until then, it quietly keeps the whole neighbourhood alive.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what makes the Sun a star and how its energy is made, then explain why it looks yellow and what will happen to it in five billion years.

name: What the Sun Is Made Of
teaser: The Sun is a giant ball of gas, and its recipe is simple: about 73 percent hydrogen, 25 percent helium, and a pinch of everything else - oxygen, carbon, iron, and all the other elements, totaling just 2 percent. This composition matches the universe's overall mix, because the Sun formed from the same cloud of gas and dust as the solar system. The hydrogen is the fuel: fusion in the core converts it to helium, releasing the energy that lights the Sun. The heavy elements, made by earlier generations of stars, are the seeds of planets and life. When we look at the Sun, we are seeing the universe's standard stellar recipe.

exploreAction.targetName: Find out what the Sun is made of
exploreAction.instruction: Find out what the Sun is mostly made of and how nuclear fusion works in its core, then explain why it shines steadily instead of exploding.

name: Layers of the Sun
teaser: Light born in the Sun's core takes a shockingly long road to the surface. A photon wanders through the dense radiative zone, bouncing off particles for tens of thousands of years, before rising through the churning convection zone — currents like a pot of boiling water. Finally it reaches the photosphere, the visible 'surface' we see, then streams out through the thin chromosphere and the ghostly corona. The corona is the strangest part: a tenuous haze of gas at over a million degrees, mysteriously hotter than the surface below it.

exploreAction.instruction: Explore the Sun's layers from the core out to the corona, then explain why the corona is hotter than the surface and what that mystery suggests.

name: Sunspots and Solar Storms
teaser: Sunspots are cooler, darker patches on the Sun's face, caused by twisted magnetic fields that poke through the surface and block rising heat. A large sunspot is bigger than Earth and can last for weeks. Watching them drift across the Sun's disk reveals its rotation, and their numbers swell and fade on an 11-year cycle — the solar cycle. At the cycle's peak, the Sun bristles with spots and hurls out violent flares; at the minimum, its face can be almost blank for months.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sunspots form and how solar flares and coronal mass ejections affect Earth, then explain what auroras have to do with them.

name: The Solar Wind
teaser: The solar wind is a constant breeze of charged particles - mostly protons and electrons - streaming off the Sun at speeds of up to 900 kilometers per second. It fills the entire solar system, creating a bubble called the heliosphere around the Sun. The solar wind is responsible for the tails of comets, which always point away from the Sun, and it sculpts the atmospheres of planets. When it hits Earth's magnetic field, it creates the auroras and, when gusty, can disrupt satellites and power grids. The wind is an outflow of the Sun's corona, heated to a million degrees. Even at the edge of interstellar space, the Voyager probes still detect the Sun's breath.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the solar wind and how it shapes the solar system, then explain how it creates comet tails and the heliosphere.

name: The Sun's Life Cycle
teaser: The Sun is about halfway through its roughly 10-billion-year life. It formed 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust, and for the last four billion years it has quietly fused hydrogen into helium in its core. In about five billion years that fuel runs low: the core shrinks, the outer layers balloon, and the Sun becomes a red giant so vast it may engulf Mercury, Venus and perhaps Earth. Then it will shed its glowing outer layers and fade into a white dwarf.

exploreAction.instruction: Follow the Sun's life from a collapsing cloud to a red giant to a white dwarf, then explain why it will not explode as a supernova.

name: Solar Eclipses
teaser: A total solar eclipse is the sky's greatest spectacle, and it exists only because of a staggering cosmic coincidence: the Moon is about 400 times smaller than the Sun but also about 400 times closer, so they appear the same size in our sky. When the alignment is perfect, the Moon covers the Sun's disk completely, day plunges into twilight, and the Sun's wispy corona blazes around the black disc. Animals behave as if night fell, and temperatures drop. Totality lasts only minutes — and the shadow's path is just a few hundred kilometres wide.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how and why solar eclipses happen and why they are rare at any one spot, then explain the difference between total, partial and annular eclipses.

name: Lunar Eclipses
teaser: When the Moon passes through Earth's shadow, it doesn't go dark — it turns a dramatic shade of red. The colour comes from sunlight filtering through Earth's atmosphere: the same scattering that makes sunsets red paints the eclipsed Moon with the light of all the world's sunrises and sunsets at once. Lunar eclipses are safe to watch with the naked eye and visible from anywhere on the night side of Earth, which is why they feel more intimate than their solar cousins. They happen only when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up at a full Moon.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out why a lunar eclipse turns the Moon red and why they are easier to see than solar eclipses, then explain the geometry behind them.

name: Why We Have Seasons
teaser: Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted 23.5 degrees, not because of how close we are to the Sun. As Earth orbits, the northern hemisphere tilts toward the Sun in June, getting more direct sunlight and longer days - summer. In December it tilts away, receiving less light - winter. The southern hemisphere experiences the opposite, which is why Christmas in Australia falls in summer. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January, at perihelion, yet that is winter in the north, proof that distance is not the driver. The tilt also produces the equinoxes and solstices, the milestones that mark the turning year.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Earth's axial tilt creates the seasons, then explain why summer and winter are opposite in the two hemispheres.

name: Equinoxes and Solstices
teaser: Twice a year, at the equinoxes, Earth's tilt points sideways relative to the Sun, and day and night are almost exactly equal across the whole planet. Twice a year, at the solstices, one pole leans its maximum toward the Sun, giving us the longest and shortest days of the year. These four moments mark the Sun's annual path through our sky, and ancient cultures built entire monuments — from Stonehenge to the pyramids — to track them. The word 'solstice' means 'Sun stands still', because the Sun seems to pause at its extremes.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out what an equinox and a solstice are and when they happen each year, then explain how different cultures have marked them.

name: Zodiacal Light
teaser: Far from city lights, just after dusk or before dawn, a faint, pyramid-shaped glow may rise from the horizon. That's the zodiacal light — sunlight scattered by trillions of tiny dust grains shed by comets and asteroids, all lying in the same flat plane as the planets. It's brightest in spring evenings and autumn mornings, when the dust band stands nearly vertical. In truly dark skies it's unmistakable: a ghostly pillar of light reaching halfway up the sky, the oldest leftover of the solar system's formation.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the faint zodiacal light that appears before dawn, then explain what causes it and when and where it is best seen.

name: Supermoons
teaser: When a full Moon coincides with perigee — the closest point in its elliptical orbit — we get a supermoon: up to 14 percent bigger and 30 percent brighter than a full Moon at the far end of its orbit. The effect is real but subtler than the hype: a size change that most people struggle to notice without comparison photos. Supermoons come in clusters of two or three, since the lunar orbit drifts in an 18-year cycle, and they're a lovely excuse to simply look up.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what a supermoon is and why the Moon sometimes looks bigger and brighter, then explain why the change is easy to overestimate.

name: Blue Moons
teaser: A blue moon isn't blue. The name goes to the second full Moon within a single calendar month, which happens only every two to three years because the lunar cycle runs about 29.5 days. The phrase 'once in a blue moon' survived for centuries as an idiom before astronomers adopted it as a label. Genuinely blue-tinted Moons are far rarer — they require volcanic ash or wildfire smoke high in the atmosphere to scatter away red light, leaving only blue. It happened famously after the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out what a blue moon really is and why the phrase is misleading, then explain how often they appear.

name: Phases of the Moon
teaser: The Moon doesn't change shape — it changes position. As it orbits Earth, we see different fractions of its sunlit half: the slender waxing crescent, the half-lit first quarter, the brilliant full Moon, then the waning gibbous shrinking back toward new. The full cycle takes 29.5 days, and that rhythm is the root of our word 'month'. The new Moon is hidden in the Sun's glare, and a crescent Moon near the horizon is the perfect target for a first look through binoculars — the 'old Moon in the new Moon's arms' glow is visible in the dark part of the disc.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why the Moon appears to change shape over a month, then explain the difference between waxing and waning and what a new moon is.

name: Tides and the Moon
teaser: Twice a day, almost everywhere on Earth, the ocean rises and falls — and the Moon is doing the pulling. Its gravity raises a bulge of water on the near side of Earth while a counterbalancing bulge forms on the far side, and Earth's rotation sweeps those two bulges past every coastline. When the Sun lines up with the Moon, their pulls combine into extra-high spring tides; when they sit at right angles, we get gentler neap tides. The Moon slowly slows Earth's spin this way, drifting a few centimetres farther away each year.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the Moon's gravity creates ocean tides and why there are two high tides a day, then explain what spring and neap tides are.

name: Why the Moon Looks Big at the Horizon
teaser: A full Moon rising behind the horizon looks enormous — like a dinner plate — yet hours later, high in the sky, it looks small. But the Moon's actual size doesn't change. It's the famous moon illusion: when the Moon is near the horizon, your brain compares it to familiar objects like trees and buildings and unconsciously magnifies it. High in the sky, with nothing to compare it against, it shrinks back to normal. Photograph the Moon in both positions and you'll find they're identical.

exploreAction.instruction: Investigate why the Moon looks enormous near the horizon and small overhead, then explain the illusion that tricks your brain.

name: The Far Side of the Moon
teaser: There is no permanently dark side of the Moon — every part gets two weeks of sunlight followed by two weeks of night. What we call the dark side is really the far side, the hemisphere that always faces away from Earth because the Moon rotates in lockstep with its orbit. Humanity first saw it in 1959, when a Soviet probe photographed it, revealing rugged highlands very different from the near side's smooth seas. The far side is also the quietest place in the solar system for radio astronomy.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out why we always see the same face of the Moon and what the far side looks like, then explain the difference between the dark side and the far side.

name: How the Moon Was Made
teaser: The leading theory of the Moon's birth is a colossal smash-up. About 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized world named Theia crashed into the young Earth with such violence that vaporized rock sprayed into orbit and slowly clumped into the Moon. The model explains why lunar rock resembles Earth's mantle, why the Moon's core is small, and why Earth spins fast on a tilted axis. Samples brought back by Apollo astronauts continue to test the story, with hints that Theia's debris may still be buried deep inside Earth today.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the leading theory of how the Moon formed from a giant impact, then explain the evidence that supports it.

name: Lunar Regolith
teaser: The Moon has no air or wind, so nothing erodes its surface — which is why astronaut footprints from the Apollo era will survive for millions of years. The ground itself is a layer of loose rubble called regolith, pulverized by billions of years of micrometeorite impacts. It's abrasive, clinging dust that plagued the astronauts' equipment. Hidden inside it, in permanently shadowed polar craters, lies something precious: water ice, a potential drinking supply and rocket fuel for future lunar bases.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what lunar regolith is and how it formed, then explain why moon dust is sharp and why it was a problem for Apollo.

name: Moonquakes
teaser: The Moon trembles — with moonquakes. Some are triggered by the pull of Earth's gravity flexing the lunar crust as the Moon orbits; others come from impacts, and a few shallow ones suggest the Moon's interior is still settling. Seismometers left behind by Apollo astronauts recorded thousands of quakes, and they're gentle by Earth standards. But without an atmosphere and water to damp vibrations, a moonquake can shake for many minutes, like a struck bell — a strange, slow shuddering unique to the airless Moon.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out what moonquakes are and what triggers them, then explain how they differ from earthquakes on Earth.

name: Mercury: Planet of Extremes
teaser: Mercury is a world of brutal extremes. With almost no atmosphere to hold heat, its sunlit side bakes at about 430 degrees Celsius — hot enough to melt lead — while the nightside plunges to minus 180. One full day on Mercury lasts 176 Earth days, spanning two of its 88-day years. Yet radar has revealed something surprising: ice lurks in permanently shadowed craters at its poles, protected from the Sun forever. Mercury is also the fastest planet, sprinting around the Sun at nearly 50 km per second.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Mercury has the wildest temperature swings in the solar system, then explain how a day on Mercury can last two Mercury years.

name: Seeing Mercury and Venus in Phases
teaser: Seen through a telescope, Mercury and Venus do something the outer planets never do: they show phases, just like the Moon. Because their orbits lie inside Earth's path, we catch them at different angles — thin crescents when they pass between us and the Sun, near-full disks when they loop behind it. Galileo watched Venus's phases in 1610 and realized it must orbit the Sun, not Earth, delivering a fatal blow to the old Earth-centred model of the cosmos. Four centuries later, the same trick helps astronomers find planets around other stars.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out why Mercury and Venus show phases like the Moon, then explain how observing them helped Galileo prove the planets orbit the Sun.

name: Venus: The Cloud World
teaser: Venus is wrapped in dazzling, unbroken clouds that reflect about 70 percent of sunlight — which is why it outshines everything in the night sky except the Moon. Up close, the beauty is deceptive: the clouds are droplets of sulfuric acid, driven by winds of hundreds of kilometres per hour. The cloud tops are its only visible face, hiding a hellish surface beneath. In the right telescope view, Venus can even show a delicate crescent, and on rare nights you can see it through a thin veil of haze.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why Venus is the hottest planet even though Mercury is closer to the Sun, then explain the runaway greenhouse effect.

name: Venus's Crushing Atmosphere
teaser: Venus wears an atmosphere so thick it's like standing at the bottom of the ocean. The surface pressure is about 92 times Earth's — roughly the crush of being a kilometre underwater — and the air is almost pure carbon dioxide, trapping heat in a runaway greenhouse effect. The result is the hottest surface of any planet: around 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead, and hotter than Mercury despite Venus being farther from the Sun. Soviet landers survived only about an hour there before being crushed and cooked.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what the atmosphere of Venus is made of and why it crushes spacecraft, then explain the sulfuric acid clouds and lightning.

name: Venus Spins Backward
teaser: Venus is the slowest spinner in the solar system. It rotates so lazily that one Venusian day lasts 243 Earth days — longer than its 225-day year — and it spins backwards, so the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east. No one knows exactly why; a giant ancient impact or long-term tidal friction from the Sun are the leading guesses. Either way, a visitor standing on Venus would watch the Sun creep across the sky once every 117 Earth days, and the winds at the cloud tops whip around the planet in just four days.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out why Venus rotates backward and so slowly, then explain what a day and a year mean there.

name: Mars: The Red Planet
teaser: Mars is red because it's rusty. Iron in its rocks reacted with oxygen and water billions of years ago to form iron oxide — the same chemistry that stains old metal — and wind has ground that rust into a fine dust coating the whole planet. The dust is so pervasive it colours the sky pink and drives global storms that can blanket everything for weeks. Underneath, Martian rocks are actually grey. NASA rovers have found that the rust dust carries secrets: minerals that only form in the presence of ancient water.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Mars looks red and what that color says about its surface, then explain what the planet was like billions of years ago.

name: Olympus Mons
teaser: Olympus Mons is the tallest volcano in the solar system — about 22 kilometres high, nearly three times the height of Everest, and so wide it would cover the whole of France. It grew so enormous because Mars has no plate tectonics: the hot spot stayed in one place for billions of years, piling lava into a single towering shield. Its slopes are so gentle you could hike to the summit without noticing, and the caldera at the top is itself the size of a small country. It last erupted maybe a few million years ago — recent enough that it could erupt again.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Olympus Mons and why it grew so enormous, then explain how Mars could once have had erupting volcanoes.

name: Valles Marineris
teaser: Valles Marineris is a canyon system that dwarfs anything on Earth: about 4,000 kilometres long, stretching a quarter of the way around Mars, and up to 7 kilometres deep — the Grand Canyon could be dropped inside it several times over. It's not a river valley; it's a giant rift in the crust, likely torn open as the volcanic Tharsis region swelled and cracked the ground. The canyon's layered walls expose a visible record of Martian history, and its floor holds sediments that could preserve evidence of ancient life.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Valles Marineris and how it formed, then explain why it dwarfs Earth's Grand Canyon.

name: Water on Mars
teaser: Billions of years ago, Mars was wet. Spacecraft have found dried river valleys, lake beds, river deltas and minerals that only form in liquid water — evidence that rivers once flowed and a vast ocean may have covered the north. Most of that water is gone, lost to space or locked underground as ice, but the poles still hold ice caps and buried glaciers have been detected across the planet. Rovers have even found mud cracks and pebbles smoothed by flowing water. Mars was once Earth-like; the question is what happened to it.

exploreAction.instruction: Investigate the evidence that Mars once had rivers, lakes and oceans, then explain where that water went.

name: Mars's Polar Caps
teaser: Mars wears bright white caps at both poles, but they're not pure water ice. Each cap has a permanent water-ice layer underneath, covered by a seasonal blanket of frozen carbon dioxide — dry ice — that grows in winter and mostly vanishes in spring, extending up to a third of the way toward the equator at its peak. As spring sunlight hits the dry ice, it sublimates straight to gas, carving strange spider-like channels and fan-shaped streaks in the ground. The caps hold enough water ice that if it melted, it could cover Mars in a shallow ocean.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out what the polar caps of Mars are made of and how they change with the seasons, then explain why they matter for future missions.

name: Phobos: The Doomed Moon
teaser: Phobos is Mars's larger moon, a lumpy, potato-shaped rock only about 22 kilometres across, pocked by craters and strange grooves. It orbits so close and so fast that it zips around Mars three times a day and rises in the west, setting in the east. And it's doomed: tidal forces are dragging it inward at about two metres per century. Within roughly 50 million years, it will either shatter into a ring of rubble or crash into the red planet's surface.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Phobos and why it is slowly spiraling toward Mars, then explain when it will break apart or crash.

name: Deimos: A Tiny Companion
teaser: Deimos, the smaller and more distant of Mars's two moons, is a smooth-looking grey rock about 12 kilometres across — so small that from Mars it appears as a bright star, not a moon. It's thought to be a captured asteroid, like its sibling Phobos, and its surface is covered in a thick layer of dust that has filled in most of its craters. Because it orbits slowly, taking 30 hours to circle Mars, it rises and sets only every couple of days.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Deimos and how it differs from Phobos, then explore the idea that both moons may be captured asteroids.

name: Jupiter's Great Red Spot
teaser: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has been raging for at least 350 years — we've watched it continuously since 1830, and it may be far older. It's an anticyclone spinning counterclockwise, with winds at its edge reaching 400 km/h. The spot has been shrinking over the past century, from about twice Earth's width down to just over one, and no one knows if it will eventually vanish. Its red colour likely comes from chemicals churned up from deeper in the atmosphere.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what the Great Red Spot is and how long it has been raging, then explain why it has been shrinking.

name: Jupiter's Belts and Zones
teaser: Jupiter's stripes are flowing bands of cloud — light 'zones' and dark 'belts' that wrap the planet and drift at different speeds in opposite directions. The light zones are cooler, ammonia-ice clouds rising high; the darker belts are warmer regions where those clouds sink. Adjacent bands shear past each other, creating turbulent swirls and eddies at their borders. Jupiter also rotates faster than any other planet, spinning once every 9.9 hours, and that furious spin stretches the bands into crisp, parallel ribbons.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why Jupiter is striped with belts and zones, then explain what drives the planet's powerful jet streams.

name: Jupiter's Magnetic Field
teaser: Jupiter has the largest magnetic field of any planet — so immense that if you could see it, it would appear bigger than the Sun in our sky. It's generated by swirling liquid metallic hydrogen deep inside the planet, and it traps radiation into belts far more intense than Earth's Van Allen belts. That radiation is so harsh it would be lethal to unshielded humans in minutes, and it's a constant headache for the spacecraft that visit. The magnetosphere also feeds the spectacular auroras at Jupiter's poles.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out how Jupiter's magnetic field works and why it is so strong, then explain what causes its enormous auroras.

name: Io: The Volcano Moon
teaser: Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system — hundreds of volcanoes erupting plumes hundreds of kilometres into space. The energy comes from tidal squeezing: Jupiter's gravity and the pull of nearby moons constantly flex Io's interior, heating it like a squeezed rubber ball. The surface is painted in yellow, red and white by sulfur compounds, with lava lakes and calderas instead of craters. Voyager caught the first eruption in 1979; the Juno mission still watches the moon's restless face today.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why Io is covered in active volcanoes, then explain the tidal heating that fuels them.

name: Europa's Hidden Ocean
teaser: Beneath Europa's cracked, icy surface almost certainly lies a global ocean of liquid water, maybe twice the volume of all Earth's oceans. The ice shell is perhaps 15 to 25 kilometres thick, and Jupiter's gravity flexes it, keeping the water beneath warm enough to stay liquid. Where the ice is thin, reddish-brown material has been detected — possibly salts or even organic compounds from below. That combination of water, chemistry and energy makes Europa one of the most promising places to hunt for life beyond Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Europa's subsurface ocean and the evidence for it, then explain why scientists think it could host life.

name: Ganymede: The Giant Moon
teaser: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system — bigger than the planet Mercury — and the only moon with its own magnetic field. Its surface shows two very different faces: ancient, dark, cratered terrain and brighter, younger regions scarred by grooves from crustal shifting. Beneath the surface, spacecraft evidence suggests a buried saltwater ocean, stacked between layers of ice. Ganymede is so big that it would be considered a planet if it orbited the Sun instead of Jupiter.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Ganymede, the largest moon in the solar system, then explore its magnetic field and possible underground ocean.

name: Callisto: The Cratered Relic
teaser: Callisto is the most heavily cratered world we know — its ancient surface records the full bombardment of the solar system's early history, unchanged for four billion years. Because it sits outside Jupiter's harshest radiation belts, its ice-and-rock crust has never been reworked by internal heat like its siblings'. Callisto is about the size of Mercury and may hide a subsurface ocean too. Some scientists argue it's the best candidate for a future crewed base: far from the radiation, with water ice for the taking.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Callisto is so heavily cratered and what its ancient surface tells us, then explain why it is a candidate for a future base.

name: Jupiter's Faint Rings
teaser: Jupiter does have rings — faint, dusty and easy to miss. Unlike Saturn's bright icy bands, Jupiter's rings are made of microscopic dust knocked off its inner moons by meteorite impacts, and they glow faintly in sunlight. There are four main components: a thick inner halo, a main ring and two gossamer rings. They were discovered only in 1979, when Voyager 1 flew past and photographed them edge-on. Every so often, material blasted from the volcanic moon Io feeds fresh dust into the ring system.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover that Jupiter has rings and why they are hard to see, then explain how they are created and sustained.

name: Saturn's Rings
teaser: Saturn's rings are the most beautiful structure in the solar system — billions of chunks of water ice, from dust grains to house-sized boulders, circling in a band 280,000 kilometres wide yet only tens of metres thick in places. Each ring orbits at its own speed, and gaps, waves and braids reveal the gravitational tug of moons. The rings are almost certainly not as old as Saturn: they may have formed from a shattered moon or comet within the last 100 million years, and they will eventually fade away.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what Saturn's rings are made of and how wide they stretch, then explain why they are so thin and bright.

name: How Saturn's Rings Formed
teaser: Saturn's rings are so thin, bright and young-looking that they probably formed recently in cosmic terms — perhaps when a moon or comet strayed too close and was torn apart by Saturn's gravity, or was shattered by a collision. Over time, ring particles drift inward and rain onto Saturn, so the rings are gradually vanishing — in a few hundred million years they may be gone. Cassini's final plunge in 2017 measured the infalling material and confirmed the rings are feeding the planet.

exploreAction.targetName: Find out where the rings came from
exploreAction.instruction: Investigate the leading ideas for how Saturn's rings formed, then explain why they may be much younger than the planet.

name: Saturn Would Float
teaser: Saturn is the least dense planet in the solar system — so light that it would float in a giant bathtub, if you could find one big enough. Its average density is lower than water because the planet is mostly hydrogen and helium, compressed only gently by its gravity. Saturn spins so fast, once every 10.7 hours, that its equator bulges outward and the planet looks visibly squashed at the poles. The low density is why it's sometimes called the 'ringed ball of fluff'.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why Saturn is the least dense planet and whether it could really float, then explain what that reveals about its interior.

name: Titan: A World of Lakes
teaser: Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere — a hazy orange shroud of nitrogen four times denser than Earth's air, hiding the surface from view. Beneath it lie lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane, the only known bodies of surface liquid beyond Earth, and rain made of hydrocarbons instead of water. It's frigid, around minus 179 degrees, yet in many ways it's the most Earth-like world we know. NASA's Dragonfly mission will send a rotorcraft there to explore the dunes and lakes in the 2030s.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Titan's lakes, rivers and rain made of methane, then explain why it is seen as one of the best places to look for life.

name: Enceladus's Geysers
teaser: Enceladus is a small moon of Saturn, just 500 kilometres across, with a bright, frozen surface — and it's alive with geysers. Huge plumes of water vapor and ice particles erupt from cracks near its south pole, shooting hundreds of kilometres into space and feeding Saturn's faint E ring. The water comes from a subsurface ocean that may be in contact with a rocky seafloor, making it one of the most promising places to search for life. Cassini flew through the plumes and tasted organic compounds in them.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the geysers of Enceladus and the ocean beneath its ice, then explain what the Cassini mission found in the plumes.

name: Mimas and the Death Star
teaser: Mimas looks uncannily like the Death Star — a small, icy moon of Saturn dominated by a giant crater called Herschel, 130 kilometres across, with walls nearly as tall as Everest. The impact that carved it must have come within a hair of shattering the moon entirely; fractures on the opposite side suggest the shock wave nearly did. Despite its cartoonish appearance, Mimas is only about 400 kilometres across, and its interior may hide a surprising secret: an ocean, hinted at by its wobble as it orbits Saturn.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why Mimas resembles the Death Star and what its giant Herschel crater tells us about its violent past.

name: Iapetus: The Two-Toned Moon
teaser: Iapetus is one of the strangest moons of Saturn: its trailing hemisphere is bright as snow, while its leading hemisphere is dark as coal — one of the most extreme colour contrasts in the solar system. The dark side is probably coated by dust from an outer moon, which absorbs sunlight, warms the surface, and makes the ice beneath sublimate away, darkening it further. Iapetus also has an enormous equatorial ridge that makes it look like a walnut, and its orbit is steeply tilted, suggesting a violent past.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Iapetus has one dark hemisphere and one bright one, then explore the ridge that wraps around its equator.

name: Tethys and Rhea
teaser: Tethys and Rhea are two icy moons of Saturn, each with a claim to fame. Tethys is dominated by Ithaca Chasma, a canyon system 2,000 kilometres long that wraps most of the way around the little moon — as if something tried to crack it in half. Rhea, a bit larger, may be the only moon in the solar system with its own faint ring system, detected as a thin band of debris around the moon. Both are frozen, ancient and quietly beautiful in Saturn's light.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the icy moons Tethys and Rhea and their surprising features, then explain how scientists map them without landing.

name: Uranus: The Tilted Planet
teaser: Uranus is the sideways planet. Its rotation axis is tilted about 98 degrees, so it essentially rolls around the Sun on its side, with its poles pointing almost straight at the star. Each pole gets 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness. The tilt may be the scar of a colossal ancient collision with an Earth-sized body. Seasons on Uranus are therefore bizarre — and the planet also has the coldest atmosphere of any planet, dropping to about minus 224 degrees.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Uranus spins on its side and how its seasons work, then explain what may have knocked it over.

name: Uranus's Vertical Rings
teaser: Uranus has a system of thin, dark rings that stand nearly vertical because the planet itself rolls on its side. They were discovered by accident in 1977, when astronomers watching a star pass behind Uranus noticed it blinked several times before the planet arrived — the star was being occulted by rings. The rings are narrow, made of dark, sooty material, and likely quite young. Some of them are shepherded by small moons, and Voyager 2 photographed them in detail on its 1986 flyby.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Uranus's rings differ from Saturn's and why they appear vertical, then explain when they are easiest to see from Earth.

name: Neptune's Supersonic Winds
teaser: Neptune is the windiest planet in the solar system, with gusts clocked at up to 2,100 km/h — faster than the speed of sound on Earth. Even though it's the farthest planet from the Sun and receives almost no solar energy, its atmosphere churns violently, driven by internal heat left over from its formation. Dark storms appear and vanish on its blue face, including a Great Dark Spot seen by Voyager 2 in 1989. Neptune's winds, its azure colour and its frantic weather make it one of the most beautiful planets.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system despite being so far from the Sun, then explain what powers them.

name: Neptune Found by Math
teaser: Neptune is the only planet found by mathematics before it was seen through a telescope. In the 1840s, astronomers noticed Uranus's orbit wobbled as if something were tugging on it, and two mathematicians — Urbain Le Verrier and John Couch Adams — independently calculated where the unseen planet should be. When telescopes turned to that spot in 1846, Neptune was there, almost exactly as predicted. It's an astonishing victory of Newtonian physics, and the planet's great moon Triton was found just weeks later.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Neptune was found with mathematics before it was seen, then explain why that made it a landmark of science.

name: Triton: The Backward Moon
teaser: Triton is Neptune's largest moon, and it's an interloper: it orbits backwards, against Neptune's rotation, the clear signature of a captured Kuiper Belt object. At minus 235 degrees it's one of the coldest places in the solar system, yet it's geologically alive — nitrogen geysers erupt from its frozen surface, painting dark streaks across the ice. It has a thin atmosphere and a bizarre 'cantaloupe' terrain of dimpled ice. Triton's retrograde orbit also means it's slowly spiraling inward, doomed to be torn apart by Neptune's gravity.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Triton's backward orbit and nitrogen geysers, then explain why it is thought to be a captured Kuiper Belt object.

name: Pluto's Heart
teaser: When New Horizons flew past Pluto in 2015, it revealed a heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice called Tombaugh Regio — the most recognizable feature on the dwarf planet. The plain is remarkably smooth and young, and it's kept that way by slow convection in the nitrogen ice. The heart is split into two lobes: one bright, one darker, with mountains of water ice as tall as the Rockies floating on the nitrogen surface. It's a strange, active world — not the dead snowball we once imagined.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the heart-shaped plain on Pluto and what it is made of, then explain how the New Horizons mission revealed it.

name: Why Pluto Is a Dwarf Planet
teaser: In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto from planet to dwarf planet after the discovery of Eris, a similar-sized world beyond it. The new definition required a planet to clear its orbit of debris — and Pluto shares its neighbourhood with the Kuiper Belt. The decision sparked a public outcry that still simmers, but it also created a new category of 'dwarf planets' that includes Pluto, Eris, Ceres, Haumea and Makemake. Whatever its label, Pluto turned out to be a fascinating little world.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, then explain the three rules for being a full planet.

name: Ceres: The Asteroid Queen
teaser: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt, about 940 kilometres across, holding roughly a third of the belt's total mass. It's technically a dwarf planet — the only one in the inner solar system. NASA's Dawn spacecraft found bright salt deposits in Occator Crater, probably left by briny water that once erupted to the surface, and evidence of past cryovolcanoes. Ceres may still hold liquid water beneath its crust, making it a fascinating target for future missions searching for the ingredients of life.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Ceres and its bright spots and possible water, then explain why it is both an asteroid and a dwarf planet.

name: Eris and the Kuiper Belt
teaser: Eris is a distant icy world in the Kuiper Belt, slightly smaller than Pluto but more massive, discovered in 2005 by Mike Brown's team. Its discovery forced astronomers to confront a growing crowd of Pluto-sized bodies — and led directly to the 2006 decision that reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet. Eris is so far away that it takes 557 years to orbit the Sun, and it has a small moon named Dysnomia. The news that a '10th planet' had been found sent the whole solar system into a naming crisis.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Eris and how its discovery forced astronomers to rethink planets, then explore what lies in the Kuiper Belt.

name: Makemake and Haumea
teaser: Makemake and Haumea are two of the strangest dwarf planets in the Kuiper Belt. Makemake, named after a Polynesian creator god, is a reddish, frozen world with a moon found in 2016, and at times it's bright enough to spot with a good amateur telescope. Haumea is more bizarre: it spins so fast, once every four hours, that it's stretched into an egg or rugby-ball shape, and it has two moons plus a ring. Both sit far beyond Neptune, in the frozen frontier of the solar system.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the dwarf planets Makemake and Haumea, then explain why Haumea is shaped like an egg and has rings.

name: The Kuiper Belt
teaser: Beyond Neptune stretches the Kuiper Belt — a vast ring of millions of icy bodies, from dust grains to dwarf planets like Pluto, Eris, Makemake and Haumea. It's the solar system's attic, filled with leftover building blocks from its formation 4.6 billion years ago. Short-period comets like Halley's come from here, and the New Horizons spacecraft flew through it in 2015, visiting Pluto and then the distant object Arrokoth in 2019. The belt may hold hundreds of thousands of objects larger than 100 kilometres.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what the Kuiper Belt is and what lives there, then explain how Pluto relates to it.

name: The Oort Cloud
teaser: Far beyond the Kuiper Belt lies the Oort Cloud — a vast, roughly spherical shell of trillions of icy bodies surrounding the solar system at distances up to a light-year from the Sun. It's never been directly observed; we infer it exists because long-period comets, like Hale-Bopp, dive in from every direction, and only a distant shell can explain that. The cloud is thought to be leftover material from the solar system's formation, flung outward by the giant planets' gravity. It marks the true edge of the Sun's influence.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the Oort Cloud and why no one has seen it directly, then explain how it sends comets toward the Sun.

name: The Asteroid Belt
teaser: Between Mars and Jupiter orbits the asteroid belt — a ring of millions of rocky bodies, from dust grains to the dwarf planet Ceres. It's not a smashed planet, as old stories claimed; it's leftover building material from the solar system's formation, kept from clumping together by Jupiter's powerful gravity. Most asteroids are dark, cratered and ancient, unchanged for 4.5 billion years. Though the belt looks crowded in films, its objects are spread so thinly that spacecraft cross it without a second thought.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what the asteroid belt is and why it never formed into a planet, then explain how big its largest members are.

name: Types of Asteroids
teaser: Asteroids come in three main flavours. C-type asteroids are dark and carbon-rich, the most common, holding primitive material from the early solar system. S-type asteroids are stony, made of silicates and metals, and are typical of the inner belt. M-type asteroids are rarer metallic worlds, thought to be the exposed iron cores of shattered protoplanets — like the one NASA's Psyche mission is visiting. Together, they record the raw ingredients from which the planets formed.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the main types of asteroids and what they are made of, then explain why composition matters for mining and science.

name: Near-Earth Objects
teaser: Near-Earth objects are asteroids and comets whose orbits bring them within about 1.3 times Earth's distance from the Sun — which means they could, one day, hit us. Astronomers have catalogued tens of thousands of them, and none of the large ones currently threaten Earth, but the search continues. NASA and other agencies now track them obsessively, mapping orbits decades into the future. The goal is simple: find them all, long before any of them finds us.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what near-Earth objects are and how astronomers track them, then explain the difference between a threat and a meteor shower.

name: Planetary Defense
teaser: Planetary defense is the serious business of protecting Earth from asteroid impacts. The toolkit includes kinetic impactors — slamming a spacecraft into the rock to nudge its orbit, as NASA's DART mission proved in 2022 — plus gravity tractors that slowly tug an asteroid with a nearby spacecraft's gravity, and nuclear options as a last resort. The key is warning time: with years of notice, even a small nudge is enough. The dinosaurs never had a defense program; we're building one.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out how scientists plan to deflect an incoming asteroid, then explain the DART mission and what a kinetic impactor does.

name: Meteorites
teaser: Meteorites are space rocks that survive the fiery plunge through Earth's atmosphere and land on the ground. They fall everywhere, all the time — tens of thousands of tonnes each year, mostly dust — but big ones are rare and precious. Iron meteorites come from the cores of shattered asteroids, stony ones from their crusts, and some rare specimens carry organic molecules and water, hinting that impacts may have delivered the ingredients for life to early Earth. Holding a meteorite is holding a piece of the solar system's childhood.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between meteors, meteoroids and meteorites, then explain what meteorites tell us about the early solar system.

name: Shooting Stars
teaser: A shooting star isn't a star at all — it's a speck of dust, often from a comet, slamming into Earth's atmosphere at tens of kilometres per second. Friction and compression heat it until it vaporizes in a blazing streak about 80 kilometres up, and the whole flash lasts less than a second. Most are smaller than a grain of sand. On a dark night you might see a handful per hour; during a meteor shower, dozens. You're watching the solar system's dust sweep past our world.

exploreAction.instruction: Find out what a shooting star really is and why it glows, then explain the difference between a meteor and a satellite streak.

name: The Perseid Meteor Shower
teaser: Every August, Earth plows through the dusty debris trail of Comet Swift-Tuttle, and the result is the Perseids — the most beloved meteor shower of the year. It peaks around August 12, when skywatchers can see 60 to 100 shooting stars an hour from dark sites. The meteors are fast, entering at 59 km per second, and often leave persistent trains. Because the shower coincides with warm summer nights in the northern hemisphere, it's the one everyone stays up for.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Perseid meteor shower and its parent comet, then explain when and how to watch it.

name: The Leonid Meteor Storms
teaser: The Leonids are the wild child of meteor showers. Most years they're modest, but every 33 years Comet Tempel-Tuttle returns and the Earth plows through fresh debris, producing meteor storms — in 1833, 1866 and 1966, observers saw tens of thousands of shooting stars per hour, with the 1833 storm sparking the first real scientific study of meteors. The meteors are exceptionally fast, and the shower radiates from the constellation Leo, peaking each November.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the Leonids and the years when they turn into storms, then explain why the display varies from year to year.

name: Halley's Comet
teaser: Halley's Comet is the most famous comet in history — the first ever recognized as periodic, returning every 76 years on average. It last visited the inner solar system in 1986, when an armada of spacecraft including Europe's Giotto flew past its nucleus, revealing a dark, peanut-shaped core that shoots jets of gas and dust. Its appearances are woven into history: it was recorded in 1066 on the Bayeux Tapestry and greeted with fear in 1910. Mark Twain was born and died in years of its return — and predicted it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Halley's Comet and its 76-year orbit, then explain how Edmond Halley predicted its return.

name: Why Comets Have Tails
teaser: A comet develops two tails as it nears the Sun, and both always point away from it. The dust tail is broad and curved, pushed by sunlight pressure, while the ion tail is straight and blue, blown by the solar wind like a weather vane. The tails can stretch tens of millions of kilometres — far longer than the distance from Earth to the Moon — yet the comet's nucleus is a fragile ball of ice and dust just a few kilometres across. A comet is a tiny body wearing a gigantic tail.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why comet tails always point away from the Sun, then explain the difference between the dust tail and the ion tail.

name: The Heart of a Comet
teaser: The heart of a comet is its nucleus — a dark, fragile 'dirty snowball' of frozen water, carbon dioxide, methane and dust, usually just a few kilometres across. As it approaches the Sun, heat vaporizes the ices, and jets of gas and dust blast off sunlit patches, sculpting craters and cliffs. Spacecraft have visited several nuclei: Halley's was a lumpy peanut, Tempel 1 had smooth and rough regions, and Rosetta's comet 67P turned out to look like a rubber duck. The dark crust hides pristine material from the solar system's birth.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what a comet nucleus is made of and how the Rosetta mission studied one, then explain what comets reveal about the early solar system.

name: Hale-Bopp: The Great Comet
teaser: Comet Hale-Bopp put on the show of the 1990s. Discovered in 1995 by two amateur astronomers, it grew into the brightest comet in decades, easily visible to the naked eye for a record 18 months in 1996 and 1997. It had two distinct tails — a white dust tail and a blue ion tail — and was photographed by millions. It's a long-period comet from the Oort Cloud, and it won't return for about 2,500 years. Its arrival also spawned a tragic cult that believed a spaceship hid behind it.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Hale-Bopp and why it was so unusually bright and long-lived, then explain why it became one of the most seen comets ever.

name: Bolides and Fireballs
teaser: A bolide is a meteor bright enough to rival the full Moon — a fireball that can light up the landscape, cast shadows and even produce sonic booms as it tears through the atmosphere faster than sound. Some explode with a flash and a ground-shaking blast, like the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor, which was only about 20 metres across yet injured 1,500 people with shattered glass. The most dramatic bolides are fragments of asteroids that had been orbiting Earth's neighbourhood. They're a reminder that the sky isn't always quiet.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what a bolide or fireball is and how bright it can get, then explain what happens when one explodes in the atmosphere.

name: Where Meteor Showers Come From
teaser: Every meteor shower traces back to a comet. As a comet orbits the Sun, its ices vaporize and shed millions of dust grains, which spread along the orbit like a river of debris. When Earth crosses that river each year at the same place, we get a shower — the Perseids from Comet Swift-Tuttle, the Leonids from Tempel-Tuttle, the Geminids from an odd 'rock comet' called 3200 Phaethon. The shower appears to radiate from a single point because the particles all travel in parallel.

exploreAction.targetName: Find the source of meteor showers
exploreAction.instruction: Discover how comets create the debris trails behind meteor showers, then explain why the same shower returns each year.

name: Impact Craters
teaser: Every solid world in the solar system is scarred by impact craters — the Moon, Mercury, Mars, even Earth. They form when an asteroid or comet slams in at tens of kilometres per second, vaporizing on impact and excavating a bowl that can be ten times wider than the object itself. Earth's craters are hard to find because erosion and plate tectonics erase them, but we've discovered over 200, including the 160-kilometre Chicxulub structure buried in Mexico. Craters are the fingerprints of cosmic violence.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how impact craters form and what they reveal about a world's age, then explain why Earth has so few compared to the Moon.

name: The Chicxulub Impact
teaser: Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid about 10 kilometres wide slammed into what is now Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, carving a crater 180 kilometres across and ending the age of dinosaurs. The impact released the energy of billions of nuclear bombs, triggering global firestorms, a long nuclear winter and an acid rain of devastation. A layer of iridium — rare on Earth, common in asteroids — marks the impact worldwide. About 75 percent of all species died, clearing the way for the mammals that eventually became us.

exploreAction.instruction: Investigate the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs, then explain the evidence found in the Chicxulub crater.

name: The Tunguska Event
teaser: On the morning of June 30, 1908, something exploded over the remote Tunguska river in Siberia with the force of a thousand Hiroshima bombs. The blast flattened 2,000 square kilometres of forest — 80 million trees knocked over in a radial pattern — yet left no crater. The culprit is thought to be a stony asteroid about 50 to 100 metres across that exploded in mid-air before touching the ground. Eyewitnesses hundreds of kilometres away saw the flash and felt the heat; the site wasn't even explored properly until 1927.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the 1908 Tunguska explosion and the ideas for what caused it, then explain why no crater was found.

name: The Chelyabinsk Meteor
teaser: On February 15, 2013, a 20-metre asteroid entered Earth's atmosphere over Chelyabinsk, Russia, and exploded 30 kilometres up with a flash brighter than the Sun. The shockwave shattered windows across the city, injuring about 1,500 people, mostly from flying glass — the first confirmed mass injury from an asteroid in modern history. The fireball was caught on countless dashboard cameras, and fragments, including a 654-kg meteorite, were recovered from a nearby lake. It was a dramatic reminder that small impacts happen regularly and unnoticed.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the Chelyabinsk meteor event and the damage it caused, then explain why it caught everyone by surprise.

name: The Earth-Moon System
teaser: Earth and the Moon form something close to a double planet. The Moon is unusually large relative to its host — about a quarter of Earth's diameter — and unusually far away, nearly 385,000 km. Our planet's rotation and the Moon's pull are locked in a slow dance: the Moon's gravity creates tides, slows Earth's spin and raises a tidal bulge that drags the Moon into a higher orbit, drifting away about 3.8 cm per year. In a few billion years, a day will be much longer — and the Moon will no longer cover the Sun in eclipses.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Earth and the Moon interact as a system, then explain how the Moon slows Earth's rotation and stabilizes its tilt.

name: Lunar Libration
teaser: Because the Moon orbits at a slightly variable speed while rotating steadily, it appears to nod and rock — a gentle wobble called libration. Over time, this rocking lets us glimpse about 59 percent of the Moon's surface instead of the 50 percent you'd expect from perfect tidal locking. The effect is subtle, but skilled observers can spot it, seeing slightly more of the eastern or western limb as the month progresses. It's a quiet reminder that the Moon's motion is more intricate than a simple lockstep.

exploreAction.targetName: See a little more of the Moon
exploreAction.instruction: Discover lunar libration and why it lets us see slightly more than half of the Moon over time, then explain what causes the wobble.

name: Sirius: The Brightest Star
teaser: Sirius, the Dog Star, is the brightest star in Earth's night sky — outshone only by the Sun, the Moon and a few planets. It's a white, hot star just 8.6 light-years away, which is why it's so brilliant despite being fairly ordinary in size. Its name comes from the Greek for 'scorching', and its rising with the Sun in July gave the ancient Egyptians the signal for the Nile's flood — the origin of our 'dog days of summer'. Sirius also has a faint white-dwarf companion, Sirius B, orbiting it every 50 years.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why Sirius is the brightest star in our night sky and how far away it is, then explain its companion white dwarf.

name: Betelgeuse: A Dying Giant
teaser: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant marking the shoulder of Orion, and it's enormous — so big that if it replaced our Sun, it would swallow the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. It's nearing the end of its life and could explode as a supernova any time in the next 100,000 years — tomorrow, or in 10,000 years, we can't know. In late 2019 it mysteriously dimmed by 60 percent, sparking worldwide headlines about an imminent explosion; it turned out to be a dust cloud, but astronomers are watching closely.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Betelgeuse and why it dimmed so dramatically in 2019, then explain what will happen when it goes supernova.

name: Rigel: The Blue Supergiant
teaser: Rigel is the brilliant blue-white star at Orion's foot — one of the most luminous stars in our galaxy, shining with the light of about 120,000 Suns. It's a blue supergiant, much hotter and far more massive than our Sun, burning fuel so fast it will live only a few million years before ending in a spectacular supernova. Despite its brilliance, Rigel is about 860 light-years away, which means we see it as it was when Charlemagne ruled Europe. It's the seventh-brightest star in our night sky.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Rigel and why blue stars are hotter than red ones, then explain what its color says about its mass and future.

name: Polaris: The North Star
teaser: Polaris, the North Star, sits almost exactly above Earth's north pole, so it barely moves while the entire sky wheels around it. For centuries it has guided travellers, its height above the horizon matching the observer's latitude. But Polaris wasn't always the North Star and won't always be: Earth's axis slowly wobbles in a 26,000-year circle called precession, so 5,000 years ago Thuban held the role, and in about 13,000 years it will pass to Vega. Polaris is also a triple star, with two faint companions.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why Polaris appears fixed in the sky and how it is used for navigation, then explain why it will not always be the North Star.

name: Vega: The Future North Star
teaser: Vega is the brightest star in the summer sky of the northern hemisphere, part of the Summer Triangle, and one of the most studied stars in astronomy. It was the first star ever photographed, the first to have its spectrum recorded, and the reference for brightness calibration for a century. About 25 light-years away, it's surrounded by a dusty debris disk, the signature of a forming planetary system. And in about 13,000 years, thanks to Earth's wobble, Vega will take over from Polaris as our North Star.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Vega and its future role as the North Star, then explain the slow wobble of Earth's axis called precession.

name: Proxima Centauri
teaser: Proxima Centauri is the Sun's closest neighbour — a small red dwarf just 4.24 light-years away. It's so dim that it wasn't discovered until 1915, and despite its proximity, it's invisible to the naked eye. It's part of the Alpha Centauri triple system, loosely bound to two brighter stars. In 2016, astronomers found a planet in its habitable zone, Proxima b, and in 2020 hints of another. Proxima is a flare star, blasting out powerful eruptions that may strip atmospheres from its planets — a fragile, fascinating world next door.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Proxima Centauri and its planet, then explain why its small size and red color make it different from the Sun.

name: Alpha Centauri: A Triple Star
teaser: Alpha Centauri is the nearest star system to the Sun, about 4.37 light-years away, and it's a family of three. Alpha Centauri A and B are two Sun-like stars orbiting each other every 80 years, while Proxima Centauri, a faint red dwarf, orbits the pair from far away. The system is a prime target for interstellar exploration — the Breakthrough Starshot project plans to send tiny laser-sailed probes there. At its speed, a voyage would take about 20 years, and the first photograph of another star system could one day look like a postcard from Earth's backyard.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the Alpha Centauri system's three stars orbit each other, then explain why it is a target for future interstellar probes.

name: Star Colors and Temperatures
teaser: A star's colour is a direct thermometer of its surface temperature. Cool red stars glow around 3,000 degrees; yellow stars like our Sun sit near 5,500; white stars reach 10,000; and searing blue giants blaze at 30,000 degrees or more. The colour comes from the same physics that makes a piece of metal glow red, then orange, then white as it heats. Simply looking at a star's tint in binoculars reveals its temperature, age and future — blue giants burn fast and die young, while red dwarfs sip fuel for trillions of years.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what a star's color tells you about its temperature, then explain the sequence from red dwarfs to blue giants.

name: How Stars Are Classified
teaser: Astronomers sort stars by temperature using the letter sequence OBAFGKM — from scorching blue O stars down to cool red M stars. The mnemonic 'Oh Be A Fine Guy/Girl, Kiss Me' helps generations remember it. Each class has subdivisions numbered 0 to 9, so the Sun is a G2 star. The system traces back to Annie Jump Cannon, who classified over 350,000 stars by eye in the early 1900s, reading their spectra from photographic plates. Her work built the foundation of modern stellar astronomy.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the system astronomers use to classify stars by temperature, then explain what each letter in OBAFGKM stands for.

name: Red Dwarfs
teaser: Red dwarfs are the most common stars in the galaxy — about 75 percent of all stars are these small, dim, cool M-class stars. They're lightweight, maybe a third of the Sun's mass or less, which makes them extremely frugal: they fuse hydrogen so slowly that they can burn for trillions of years, far longer than the universe has even existed. None has ever died of old age. Their planets, like Proxima b, sit close in and may face constant flares, but their longevity makes them fascinating targets in the search for life.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why red dwarfs are the most abundant stars and why they burn so long, then explain whether their planets could support life.

name: White Dwarfs
teaser: White dwarfs are the cooling embers of Sun-like stars - the dense, Earth-sized cores left behind when a star sheds its outer layers. A white dwarf packs the mass of the Sun into a volume the size of Earth, making it so dense that a teaspoon of its material would weigh tons. It is no longer fusing anything; it shines from residual heat and will cool for billions of years. White dwarfs are supported by a strange quantum pressure, not by fusion, and they have a strict mass limit - about 1.4 times the Sun - beyond which they collapse or explode. Our Sun will become a white dwarf in about five billion years. These embers are the fate of most stars in the universe.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how a star's core becomes an ultra-dense white dwarf, then explain why a teaspoon weighs tons.

name: Neutron Stars
teaser: Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of massive stars that exploded as supernovae — city-sized spheres about 20 kilometres across packing more mass than the Sun. They're so dense that a sugar-cube of neutron star matter would weigh about a billion tonnes on Earth. In them, gravity has crushed protons and electrons together into neutrons. Some spin hundreds of times per second, and the strongest have magnetic fields that would erase credit cards from lunar orbit. They are the densest visible objects in the universe.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how a neutron star forms and why a teaspoon of it weighs a billion tons, then explain what makes it spin so fast.

name: Pulsars
teaser: Pulsars are rapidly spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radio waves across the sky like cosmic lighthouses. As they rotate, their beams flash past Earth with stunning regularity — the fastest spin hundreds of times per second, and their pulses are more precise than atomic clocks. The first pulsar was found in 1967 by graduate student Jocelyn Bell, who noticed a 'scruffy' signal blinking every 1.3 seconds. Pulsars are so regular they were once mistaken for alien beacons — and today they're used as cosmic clocks to detect gravitational waves.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what a pulsar is and why it appears to blink, then explain how the discovery of pulsars was once mistaken for alien signals.

name: Magnetars
teaser: Magnetars are neutron stars with the most extreme magnetic fields in the universe — a thousand trillion times stronger than Earth's. Such fields are so powerful that they warp atoms into needles and can strip electrons from matter. Magnetars occasionally unleash enormous flares that outshine every star in the galaxy for a moment, and on March 5, 1979, one sent a blast that swept past Earth, briefly disrupting satellites. Only about 30 are known — rare, terrifying objects at the edge of physics.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover magnetars and their impossibly strong magnetic fields, then explain how they are related to neutron stars.

name: Supernovae
teaser: Supernovae are the greatest explosions in the universe - the violent deaths of stars that briefly outshine entire galaxies. A single supernova releases more energy in seconds than the Sun will in its whole lifetime. There are two main kinds: core-collapse supernovae, when a massive star's core collapses and detonates, and Type Ia supernovae, when a white dwarf accumulates too much matter and blows up. Both forge heavy elements and scatter them across space, seeding future stars and planets - the gold in your jewelry and the iron in your blood were made in supernovae. The last naked-eye supernova in our galaxy was in 1604; astronomers wait for the next with telescopes ready. When a star dies this violently, it lights the universe.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what triggers a supernova and what it leaves behind, then explain why these explosions are essential for making the elements of life.

name: Novae and Supernovae
teaser: Novas and supernovas sound alike but are completely different beasts. A nova happens on a white dwarf that steals hydrogen from a companion star; the stolen fuel ignites in a surface explosion, brightening the star for weeks or months — the white dwarf survives. A supernova is vastly more powerful: the star itself is destroyed, either collapsing or detonating, releasing a million times more energy than a nova. Supernovas can be seen across the universe; novas are mostly within our own galaxy.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the difference between a nova and a supernova, then explain which one can repeat and why.

name: Star Clusters
teaser: Star clusters are families of stars born together from the same cloud of gas. Open clusters like the Pleiades hold hundreds of young, loosely bound stars, drifting apart over millions of years. Globular clusters are ancient, tightly packed balls of hundreds of thousands of stars, some over 12 billion years old — the oldest objects we can see. The difference: open clusters wander the galaxy's disk, while globulars orbit in the halo, relics of the galaxy's youth. Both are beautiful sights in any telescope.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about open and globular clusters and how they form, then explain why cluster stars share an age.

name: Nebulae
teaser: Nebulae are the glowing clouds of the cosmos - vast regions of gas and dust that come in many forms. Some are nurseries where stars are born, lit by the young stars inside them; others are the leftover shrouds of dying stars; still others are dark clouds that block the light behind them. The word comes from Latin for 'cloud,' and early astronomers used it for any fuzzy patch of sky. Modern astronomy divides nebulae by their behavior: emission nebulae glow on their own, reflection nebulae shine by scattered starlight, and dark nebulae hide the stars behind them. Nebulae are the raw material of the universe, the places where stars and planets are assembled - and some of the most beautiful objects in the sky.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what nebulae are and how they give birth to stars, then explain the difference between emission, reflection and dark nebulae.

name: Stellar Nurseries
teaser: Stars are born in stellar nurseries — cold, dense clouds of molecular gas and dust, some light-years across. A disturbance, like a shock wave from a supernova, triggers the collapse of denser knots, which heat up and ignite fusion, lighting up the cloud from within. The result is a cluster of newborn stars surrounded by glowing gas — exactly what we see in the Orion Nebula and the Eagle Nebula's Pillars of Creation. Our Sun was born in such a nursery 4.6 billion years ago, probably alongside hundreds of sibling stars.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how a cloud of gas collapses into new stars, then explain why young stars often come in clusters.

name: The Named Stars of the Sky
teaser: The names in our sky read like a history of astronomy: Betelgeuse, an Arabic phrase meaning 'armpit of the giant'; Polaris, Latin for 'pole star'; Vega, from the Arabic for 'falling eagle'. Many bright stars carry Arabic names from the Golden Age of Islamic astronomy, while the constellations themselves are Greek, Babylonian and even older. Modern catalogues added letters and numbers, and exoplanets carry names like Proxima Centauri b. Every star name is a fossil word from the cultures that mapped the heavens.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how stars get their names and why many come from Arabic, then explain the difference between a name and a catalog number.

name: Black Holes
teaser: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so intense that nothing — not even light — can escape. They form when massive stars collapse at the end of their lives, or when huge amounts of matter gather in one place. The boundary is called the event horizon, and inside it, our laws of physics break down. Despite the name, black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners; they only trap things that cross the horizon. The one at the Milky Way's centre, Sagittarius A*, weighs 4 million Suns.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what a black hole is and how its gravity works, then explain why not even light can escape it.

name: The Event Horizon
teaser: The event horizon is the boundary of a black hole — the surface of no return. Inside it, gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape, and our understanding of physics breaks down. The horizon isn't a physical surface; it's a mathematical boundary in spacetime, but it's very real in effect. Time behaves strangely there: to a distant observer, an object falling in appears to slow and freeze at the horizon, growing redder and fainter, never quite crossing — while to the falling object, the crossing is uneventful. The 2019 image of M87's black hole showed the shadow of an event horizon for the first time. It's the edge of the known universe.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what the event horizon is and what happens when you cross it, then explain why black holes are not really holes.

name: How Black Holes Form
teaser: Stellar black holes are the most common kind, born when the most massive stars — at least 20 to 25 times the Sun's mass — run out of fuel and collapse at the end of their lives. The core implodes to a point, while the outer layers explode in a supernova. The result is a black hole a few to a few dozen times the Sun's mass, hidden in space. Our galaxy likely holds millions of them, detected when they pull gas from a companion star or when two merge, ringing the fabric of spacetime with gravitational waves.

exploreAction.targetName: Learn how black holes are born
exploreAction.instruction: Find out how the collapse of a massive star can create a black hole, then explain the difference between stellar and supermassive black holes.

name: Supermassive Black Holes
teaser: Supermassive black holes are the giants at the hearts of galaxies, weighing millions to billions of times the Sun's mass. No one knows exactly how they grew so enormous — perhaps by merging smaller black holes, or by gulping gas in the early universe. The Milky Way's own, Sagittarius A*, weighs about 4 million Suns, and its 2022 image showed a glowing ring around a dark shadow. Nearly every large galaxy appears to host one, and their gravity shapes how galaxies themselves evolve.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the supermassive black holes that sit in the middle of galaxies, then explain how they grow and how we detect them.

name: Sagittarius A*
teaser: At the exact centre of the Milky Way lies Sagittarius A* — a supermassive black hole weighing about 4 million times the Sun's mass. Astronomers proved its existence by tracking stars orbiting it at blistering speeds; one, S2, whips around the black hole every 16 years. In 2022, the Event Horizon Telescope imaged it directly, showing the glowing ring of superheated gas around its shadow. Despite its vast mass, it's a relatively quiet giant — a sleeping dragon at our galaxy's heart.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the center of our galaxy, then explain how scientists photographed it.

name: Gravitational Waves
teaser: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime itself, spreading outward from accelerating masses like ripples on a pond. They were predicted by Einstein in 1916 as a consequence of general relativity: when masses accelerate — two black holes spiraling together, a supernova's core collapsing — spacetime stretches and compresses in waves travelling at light speed. They're unimaginably faint, so it took a century to build detectors sensitive enough: LIGO heard its first signal in 2015, from two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away. Since then, dozens of detections have opened a new window on the universe. We can now hear the cosmos, not just see it.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover gravitational waves and how colliding black holes make them, then explain how LIGO measures these tiny ripples.

name: LISA: Listening in Space
teaser: LISA — the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna — is a planned space observatory that will listen for gravitational waves from space, a million times more sensitive than ground detectors. It consists of three spacecraft flying in a triangle millions of kilometres apart, using lasers to measure tiny ripples in spacetime. Where LIGO hears brief chirps, LISA will track the slow spiral of supermassive black holes and exotic binaries for years. Slated for launch in the 2030s, it promises to open a whole new window on cosmic collisions.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the planned LISA observatory and how it will detect ripples in space from across the universe, then explain why it needs three spacecraft.

name: Dark Matter
teaser: Dark matter is the invisible substance that makes up about 27% of the universe — five times more abundant than the ordinary matter we're made of. It doesn't emit, absorb or reflect light, so we can't see it; we know it exists from its gravity. Galaxies spin too fast to stay bound by their visible stars alone, and light from distant galaxies bends more than it should — both effects demand extra mass we can't see. Dark matter likely consists of undiscovered particles, and experiments worldwide are hunting them. It's the scaffolding on which galaxies and the cosmic web are built. The universe's structure — and our existence — depends on matter we've never directly seen.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what dark matter is thought to be and why astronomers are sure it exists, then explain the evidence from galaxy rotation.

name: Dark Energy
teaser: Dark energy is the name for the mysterious force driving the universe's expansion to accelerate. Discovered in 1998 by two teams measuring distant supernovae, it behaves like a repulsive gravity, pushing space apart faster and faster. It makes up about 68% of the universe's energy budget — the dominant ingredient of reality — yet we don't know what it is. The leading candidate is the cosmological constant, a property of empty space itself, though its predicted strength doesn't match observation by a factor of 10 to the power 120. Dark energy decides the universe's ultimate fate: if it keeps accelerating, the cosmos will expand forever, growing cold, dark and empty.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover dark energy and the evidence that the universe's expansion is speeding up, then explain why it makes up most of the cosmos.

name: The Cosmic Microwave Background
teaser: The cosmic microwave background is the oldest light in the universe — the afterglow of the Big Bang, released about 380,000 years after the cosmos began when it cooled enough for atoms to form and light to travel freely. It now fills all of space as a faint microwave glow at 2.7 degrees above absolute zero, and it's the same in every direction. It was discovered by accident in 1964 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, who heard a stubborn hiss in their radio antenna and eventually realized it was the birth-light of the universe. The background's tiny temperature ripples are the seeds of galaxies. It's the most perfect evidence for the Big Bang.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how faint microwaves from the Big Bang still bathe the sky, then explain what they reveal about the early universe.

name: The Big Bang
teaser: The Big Bang theory says the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in an incredibly hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since. It's not an explosion in space — it's the expansion of space itself, everywhere at once. Three lines of evidence seal it: the expansion of galaxies, the cosmic microwave background afterglow, and the precise mix of light elements like hydrogen and helium. The theory says nothing about what came 'before' — time itself may have begun there.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what the Big Bang really was and what happened in its first moments, then explain why it was not an explosion in space.

name: Cosmic Inflation
teaser: Cosmic inflation is the theory that, in the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang, the universe expanded faster than the speed of light — ballooning from a subatomic speck to astronomical size in a trillionth of a trillionth of a second. Proposed in 1980 by Alan Guth, it solves deep puzzles: why the universe is so uniform, why it's so flat, and why we see no exotic relics. Inflation stretched tiny quantum fluctuations into the seeds of galaxies. It's the most successful theory of the early universe, though its mechanism remains unknown. The cosmos we see was inflated from a quantum seed in a flash beyond imagination.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about cosmic inflation and why the early universe expanded faster than light, then explain what it solves.

name: The Expanding Universe
