teaser: When astronomers say the universe is expanding, they don't mean galaxies are flying through space — they mean space itself is stretching, carrying galaxies apart like dots on an inflating balloon. Every distant galaxy is moving away from us, and the farther it is, the faster it recedes. The expansion began with the Big Bang and, surprisingly, is accelerating, driven by dark energy. In the far future, galaxies will be so far apart that each will sit alone in a dark, empty cosmos.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the evidence that the universe is expanding, then explain redshift and how Edwin Hubble measured it.

name: Redshift
teaser: Redshift is the cosmic ruler: the more a galaxy's light is stretched toward red, the farther away it is. It works through the Doppler effect — receding objects stretch light — combined with the universe's expansion stretching space itself. Astronomers measure redshift by comparing a galaxy's spectral lines with laboratory values, and the number z expresses the stretch. A galaxy at z=1 has its light doubled in wavelength and is about 10 billion light-years away; the most distant galaxies exceed z=10, seen as they were 13 billion years ago. Redshift isn't just distance — it's cosmic time travel, measured in stretched light.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what redshift is and how it tells us how far away things are, then explain the difference between redshift and blueshift.

name: Hubble's Law
teaser: Hubble's Law is the simple, profound rule that the farther a galaxy is from us, the faster it's moving away. Edwin Hubble announced the relationship in 1929, using distances to galaxies measured by Henrietta Leavitt's Cepheid method, and it became the first observational evidence that the universe is expanding. The constant connecting distance and speed is the Hubble constant, and pinning down its exact value — with a nagging tension between different measurements — is one of cosmology's liveliest debates today.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Hubble's law and the discovery that made Edwin Hubble famous, then explain what the constant tells us about the universe's age.

name: How Old Is the Universe?
teaser: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old — and astronomers know this with remarkable precision. They measure it three independent ways: the expansion rate of the universe, the ages of the oldest stars, and the subtle temperature patterns in the cosmic microwave background. All three agree on 13.8 billion years, give or take a few tens of millions. It means the universe has existed about three times longer than Earth, and its observable edge is 13.8 billion light-years away in every direction.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how astronomers measure the universe's age, then explain why the expansion rate and the CMB both point to 13.8 billion years.

name: The Cosmic Web
teaser: On the largest scales, the universe isn't a random smear of galaxies — it's a web. Galaxies string along vast filaments of dark matter, separated by enormous empty voids, with dense clusters at the intersections. It looks like the neural network of the brain or a foam of bubbles, spanning billions of light-years. The structure grew from tiny density ripples in the early universe, amplified by gravity over 13.8 billion years. Every galaxy, including ours, rides one strand of this cosmic web.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the large-scale structure of the universe and how galaxies form a web, then explain what dark matter has to do with it.

name: The Multiverse Idea
teaser: The multiverse is the idea that our universe may be just one bubble in an infinite foam of universes, each with its own laws of physics. It arises naturally from theories like cosmic inflation, which may forever spawn new universes, and from string theory's landscape of possible realities. It's a deeply controversial idea because other universes may be impossible to observe — which has some scientists calling it philosophy, not physics. Yet it offers a haunting answer to the question 'why is the universe so finely tuned for life?': because we're in one of the lucky bubbles.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the scientific ideas behind a multiverse, then explain why some physicists take it seriously and others are skeptical.

name: The Fine-Tuning Question
teaser: The constants of physics seem absurdly fine-tuned for life. If the strength of gravity, the mass of the electron, or the expansion rate of the universe differed by a hair, atoms couldn't form, stars wouldn't burn, and life couldn't exist. It's as if the universe were dialed in for us. Some see evidence of design; others invoke the multiverse, where we simply live in one of countless universes with the right settings. Either way, it's one of the deepest open questions in science: why is the universe so hospitable?

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why the universe's constants seem perfectly tuned for life, then explore the different explanations scientists debate.

name: Echoes of Inflation
teaser: If cosmic inflation really happened in the first instant of the universe, it should have left behind an echo: gravitational waves rippling through spacetime, imprinted as a swirling pattern in the cosmic microwave background. Astronomers have searched for this 'B-mode' polarization signal for decades, and in 2014 a team announced a detection that turned out to be dust in our own galaxy. The search continues with ever more sensitive telescopes. Finding it would be a direct photograph of the Big Bang's first whisper.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how scientists look for gravitational waves left over from inflation, then explain what finding them would prove.

name: The Milky Way
teaser: The Milky Way is our home galaxy — a barred spiral of between 100 and 400 billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across. We see it as a pale band of light across the night sky because we live inside its disk, looking edge-on through a sea of stars. At its centre sits a supermassive black hole, and its spiral arms are the nurseries of new stars. The Sun is about 26,000 light-years from the centre, riding the Orion Arm — a minor suburb in a vast cosmic city.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the structure of the Milky Way and where our solar system sits, then explain why it is called a barred spiral galaxy.

name: The Milky Way's Center
teaser: The heart of the Milky Way is a crowded, brilliant region in the constellation Sagittarius — a bulge of billions of old stars, glowing gas clouds and dust lanes, anchored by the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*. From dark skies, it's visible as a bright swelling of the Milky Way band, though dust hides much of it from optical view; infrared telescopes reveal a dense swarm of stars.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what lies at the center of the Milky Way, then explain why we cannot see it in visible light.

name: Andromeda: Our Sister Galaxy
teaser: Andromeda is the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away — and the farthest thing the human eye can see without a telescope. It's a spiral somewhat larger than our own, holding about a trillion stars, and it's approaching us at 110 km per second. In about 4.5 billion years, Andromeda and the Milky Way will collide and merge into a giant elliptical galaxy, reshaping our sky over hundreds of millions of years. Our descendants, if any, will watch the greatest show in cosmic history.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Andromeda and why it is the farthest thing you can see with your eyes, then explain what will happen when it collides with the Milky Way.

name: When Galaxies Collide
teaser: Galaxies collide all the time — and it's not the destructive crash you might imagine. Stars are so far apart that few ever physically touch; instead, the galaxies' gravity tears them into streams, bridges and tails of stars as they pass through each other. The gas clouds do collide, triggering bursts of new star formation. Over hundreds of millions of years, the pair merges into one larger galaxy. The Milky Way itself is the product of countless past mergers — and Andromeda is already on its way.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what happens when galaxies collide, then explain why the stars inside rarely crash into each other.

name: Spiral Galaxies
teaser: Spiral galaxies are the pinwheels of the universe — flat, rotating disks of stars, gas and dust with graceful arms sweeping out from a bright central bulge. The arms aren't solid structures but waves of density that compress gas and trigger star formation, so they glow blue with young, hot stars. About two-thirds of all galaxies in the local universe are spirals or their barred cousins. Our Milky Way and Andromeda are both barred spirals. These are the most photogenic galaxies, and the most studied.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why spiral galaxies have arms and how they stay wound, then explain the role density waves play.

name: Elliptical Galaxies
teaser: Elliptical galaxies are round or oval clouds of old stars with no spiral arms — often described as 'red and dead'. Their stars are mostly ancient and reddish, with little gas left to form new ones, so they glow with the warm light of maturity rather than the blue fire of youth. They range from dwarfs to giants far larger than the Milky Way, and the biggest, found at the centres of galaxy clusters, are the largest galaxies in the universe. Many were formed when spirals merged together.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what elliptical galaxies are and how they differ from spirals, then explain why they contain mostly old stars.

name: Irregular Galaxies
teaser: Irregular galaxies are the oddballs — shapeless, chaotic systems that follow no tidy spiral or oval pattern. Most are small and low-mass, and many have been distorted by the gravity of a larger neighbour, or are simply too young to have settled into a form. The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, visible from the southern hemisphere, are famous irregulars orbiting our own galaxy. They're often rich in gas and alive with star formation, making them favourite targets for studying how stars are born.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover irregular galaxies and what distorts them, then explain why they are often small and gas-rich.

name: The Hubble Tuning Fork
teaser: Astronomers sort galaxies using Edwin Hubble's 'tuning fork' diagram, devised in 1926. On one prong sit spirals, from tight-arm 'Sa' to loose 'Sc' forms; on the other, barred spirals, with a bar of stars through the centre; and at the handle, featureless ellipticals, from round E0 to elongated E7. Irregulars fit nowhere and hang off the diagram. Hubble's scheme turned out to be more than a filing system — it roughly tracks a galaxy's age, star formation and history of mergers.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Edwin Hubble classified galaxies by shape, then explain why the tuning fork diagram is still useful today.

name: Quasars
teaser: Quasars are the most luminous objects in the universe — brilliant beacons powered by supermassive black holes devouring matter at the centres of distant galaxies. A single quasar can outshine a trillion Suns, and they're visible billions of light-years away. When first found in the 1960s, their strange radio signals earned them the name 'quasi-stellar radio sources'. The brightest of all, 3C 273, is so far away that its light left when Earth was young. Quasars were far more common in the early universe, when black holes had more fuel.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover quasars and what powers their brilliance, then explain why seeing a quasar means looking far back in time.

name: Active Galactic Nuclei
teaser: Some galaxies have violently active hearts, known as active galactic nuclei. At the centre, a supermassive black hole is swallowing a stream of gas and stars, heating the infalling matter until it blazes in every wavelength — and sometimes blasting twin jets of plasma into space at near light speed. When the galaxy is viewed down the jet, we see a blazar; from the side, a radio galaxy. Our own Milky Way's black hole is quiet today, but it may have been an active nucleus in the past.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what makes a galaxy's core active, then explain how matter falling into a supermassive black hole blazes so brightly.

name: Galaxy Groups and Clusters
teaser: Galaxies almost never live alone — they gather in groups and clusters. Our Local Group is a small collection of a few dozen galaxies, dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda. Clusters are far grander: thousands of galaxies bound by gravity, wrapped in halos of dark matter and hot gas, like the Virgo Cluster with 1,300 members. The largest structures of all, superclusters, string galaxies along filaments across hundreds of millions of light-years. Gravity is the sculptor of these vast cosmic cities.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how galaxies group into clusters and superclusters, then explain how gravity and dark matter hold them together.

name: The Local Group
teaser: The Local Group is our cosmic neighbourhood — a gravitationally bound collection of more than 80 galaxies, spread across about 10 million light-years. Its two giants are the Milky Way and Andromeda, each with retinues of dwarf satellites; the Triangulum galaxy sits as the third-largest member. Most of the group's galaxies are tiny dwarfs, barely holding a few million stars. The group is small enough that its gravity overcomes cosmic expansion, so the Milky Way and Andromeda are still moving toward each other.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Local Group of galaxies and its members, then explain why Andromeda and the Milky Way dominate it.

name: Dwarf Galaxies
teaser: Dwarf galaxies are the most common galaxies in the universe — small systems of a few million to a few billion stars, easily outnumbered by giants. Most are faint and hard to find, which is why new ones around the Milky Way are still being discovered. They come in many forms: dwarf ellipticals, irregular dwarfs, and ultra-faint dwarfs holding just a few thousand stars. Dwarfs are living fossils of the early universe and sensitive laboratories for dark matter — and they're what most of the cosmos actually looks like.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover dwarf galaxies and why they outnumber giants, then explain what they reveal about galaxy formation.

name: Star-Forming Galaxies
teaser: Star-forming galaxies blaze with the blue light of newborn stars, often erupting at staggering rates. In 'starburst' galaxies, something — usually a merger with another galaxy — compresses the gas, igniting star formation hundreds of times faster than normal. The Milky Way forms a few Suns a year; a starburst can form hundreds. These galaxies glow brilliantly in infrared, where dust heated by young stars re-radiates its energy. Looking deep into the universe, astronomers see mostly star-forming galaxies — cosmic firecrackers of the early era.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why some galaxies form stars at furious rates, then explain what triggers a starburst.

name: The Galactic Halo
teaser: Around every galaxy hangs a faint halo — a vast, roughly spherical cloud of ancient stars and globular clusters, plus dark matter. The Milky Way's halo contains its oldest stars, some nearly as old as the universe, plus about 150 globular clusters. The halo stars are relics, formed before the disk, and many are the fossil remains of galaxies the Milky Way swallowed. The visible halo is only the tip: the dark-matter halo extends far beyond it, holding the galaxy together. What we see of a galaxy is just its bright heart.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the halo of the Milky Way and the globular clusters inside it, then explain how it helps measure the galaxy's mass.

name: The Interstellar Medium
teaser: The interstellar medium is the thin gas and dust between the stars - the universe's background substance, filling the spaces of the galaxy. It is incredibly sparse, with a few atoms per cubic centimeter in most places, yet it contains enough matter to form new stars and shape the galaxy. It comes in several phases: cold molecular clouds where stars form, warm neutral hydrogen, and hot ionized gas blown by supernovae. The dust grains within it redden and dim starlight, and its gas provides the raw material for future generations of stars and planets. The interstellar medium is not empty space but the galaxy's lifeblood, circulating between stars and the space between them.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what fills the space between stars, then explain how gas and dust recycle into new stars and planets.

name: Cosmic Dust
teaser: Cosmic dust - tiny grains of silicates, carbon, and ice a fraction of a micrometer across - is the universe's most pervasive and influential substance. Despite being almost nothing, it shapes everything: dust dims and reddens starlight, hides newborn stars, and helps gas clouds cool enough to collapse into stars. Dust grains are also the building blocks of planets, clumping together to form asteroids, comets, and worlds. They are made in the winds of dying stars and supernovae, scattered across space, and eventually incorporated into new stars and planets - which means every grain of dust in your home was once stardust. Cosmic dust is the quiet scaffolding of the universe, turning gas into stars and stars into planets.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how dust absorbs, scatters and reddens starlight, then explain why astronomers call it extinction.

name: How Galaxies Formed
teaser: Galaxies formed from the slow growth of tiny density ripples left over from the Big Bang. Gravity pulled matter into clumps, dark matter provided the scaffolding, and gas fell in, igniting the first stars within a few hundred million years. Small galaxies merged into bigger ones, feeding supermassive black holes along the way. Over 13 billion years, the process built everything from dwarf irregulars to giant ellipticals. The details are still being studied — but every galaxy, including ours, is a product of this cosmic assembly line.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the first galaxies formed after the Big Bang, then explain how mergers and gas flows build them over time.

name: The First Galaxies
teaser: The first galaxies lit up the universe only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang — small, chaotic and blazing with newly formed stars. The James Webb Space Telescope has been pushing further back than ever, finding galaxies from when the universe was just 300 million years old, far earlier than expected. These early pioneers were crucial: their starlight ended the cosmic 'dark ages' and ionized the hydrogen fog. They were smaller and more violent than modern galaxies, and they grew by merging.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how telescopes like JWST hunt the first galaxies, then explain what their light tells us about the early universe.

name: The Milky Way's Mergers
teaser: The Milky Way is a cannibal. Its halo is full of streams of stars — the shredded remains of dwarf galaxies it has swallowed over billions of years, like the Gaia-Enceladus merger about 10 billion years ago that helped build its halo and thick disk. It's currently pulling in the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy, and in about 4.5 billion years it will merge with Andromeda. Galactic mergers aren't rare accidents; they're the standard way galaxies grow. Our galaxy's past is written in the streams of stars around it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the Milky Way grew by merging with smaller galaxies, then explain the evidence like tidal streams of stars.

name: The Telescope
teaser: The telescope was invented around 1608 in the Netherlands — a humble spyglass made of two lenses in a tube, a toy that let merchants spot ships on the horizon. Word reached Galileo in Italy in 1609, and within months he had built his own and turned it to the sky, discovering mountains on the Moon, the phases of Venus and the moons of Jupiter. The instrument that began as a curiosity transformed astronomy from a pattern-watching art into a science of discovery. Four centuries later, telescopes span the Earth and orbit in space.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the first telescopes worked and what Galileo saw with them, then explain how a simple refractor bends light.

name: Refractor Telescopes
teaser: A refracting telescope gathers light with a curved glass lens at the front, bending it to a focus at the eyepiece — the classic long, slender design. Galileo's instrument and the great 19th-century giants like the Yerkes 40-inch were refractors, and they excel at crisp views of the Moon, planets and double stars. Their weakness: large lenses are heavy, expensive and suffer from colour fringing. That's why the biggest telescopes of today are all reflectors, and refractors survive mostly in amateur astronomy and small instruments.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how refractor telescopes use lenses to focus light, then explain why very large ones are hard to build.

name: Reflector Telescopes
teaser: Reflecting telescopes gather light with a curved mirror, which can be made far larger and cheaper than a lens, and they suffer no colour fringing. Isaac Newton built the first practical one in 1668, and his design — the Newtonian — is still the standard for amateurs. Modern giants like the Keck telescopes use segmented mirrors 10 metres across, and the upcoming Extremely Large Telescope will use a mirror 39 metres wide. The Hubble and James Webb space telescopes are also reflectors, catching faint light from the edge of the universe.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why most big telescopes use mirrors instead of lenses, then explain how Isaac Newton's design changed astronomy.

name: The Hubble Space Telescope
teaser: Launched in 1990, the Hubble Space Telescope orbits above Earth's blurring atmosphere and has rewritten astronomy. Its sharp images transformed nearly every field: it helped pin down the universe's age and expansion rate, photographed galaxies billions of light-years away, watched a comet crash into Jupiter, and captured the famous Pillars of Creation. Over 30 years, astronauts repaired and upgraded it five times, keeping a 1970s design cutting-edge into the 21st century. It has taken over 1.5 million observations and is arguably the most important scientific instrument ever built.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Hubble works above Earth's atmosphere and what it discovered, then explain why its location gives it such sharp views.

name: Hubble's Mirror Problem
teaser: When Hubble launched in 1990, its first images were a crushing disappointment: a mirror ground to the wrong shape left everything blurred. NASA called it 'astigmatism' — a flaw in a primary mirror just 2 microns thick in error. In 1993, astronauts performed the daring repair: five spacewalks to install corrective optics, turning the 'Hubble Trouble' into history's most successful repair job. Within weeks the telescope delivered razor-sharp images. The rescue also saved the shuttle program's reputation and proved humans could service spacecraft.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Hubble's flawed mirror was diagnosed and repaired in space, then explain why the fix was considered a triumph.

name: The James Webb Space Telescope
teaser: The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in December 2021, is the largest and most powerful space telescope ever built — a 6.5-metre gold-coated mirror made of 18 segments, designed to see in infrared. It unfolded itself in space through a nail-biting sequence of 344 steps, including a tennis-court-sized sunshield. From a million kilometres out, Webb peers at the first galaxies, watches stars being born inside dust clouds, and sniffs the atmospheres of exoplanets. Its first images in 2022 showed the universe deeper and sharper than ever before.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how JWST sees the infrared and why it orbits far from Earth, then explain what its deep images reveal.

name: Webb vs Hubble
teaser: Hubble and Webb are complementary eyes on the cosmos. Hubble, in low Earth orbit, sees mostly in visible and ultraviolet light — the colours our eyes know — and has spent 30 years delivering its iconic images. Webb, a million kilometres out, sees in infrared, the light of the early universe, which has been stretched red by cosmic expansion. Webb can see through dust clouds where stars are born; Hubble sees the glowing details. Together they cover the universe from its infancy to its present.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how JWST and Hubble differ in wavelength, size and orbit, then explain why astronomers need both.

name: Radio Astronomy
teaser: Radio astronomy listens to the universe at wavelengths invisible to our eyes. It was born by accident in 1932, when Karl Jansky, an engineer hunting static that interfered with transatlantic phone calls, discovered radio noise coming from the Milky Way itself. Today, giant dishes and arrays reveal the universe's hidden voices: pulsars ticking like clocks, jets from black holes, the faint hiss of the Big Bang's afterglow, and clouds of cold gas where stars form. Some wavelengths even pass straight through Earth's clouds, letting us see the sky in any weather.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how radio telescopes reveal invisible cosmic objects, then explain what radio waves can teach us that light cannot.

name: Arecibo Observatory
teaser: The Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico was, for 57 years, the largest single-dish radio telescope ever built — a 305-metre bowl carved into a sinkhole in the karst landscape. It starred in films like Contact and GoldenEye, sent the 1974 Arecibo Message toward star cluster M13, and discovered the first planets ever found beyond our Sun, orbiting a pulsar. Hurricane Maria and years of neglect took their toll, and in December 2020 the giant dish collapsed. Its legacy lives on in every radio astronomer who ever listened with it.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Arecibo's contributions to science and its dramatic collapse, then explain why its size made it special.

name: The Very Large Array
teaser: The Very Large Array in New Mexico is twenty-seven radio dishes, each 25 metres across, spread across the desert in a giant Y shape spanning 36 kilometres. The dishes work together as one enormous telescope, combining their signals to produce images as sharp as a dish 36 km wide could make. It's been a star of film and television — most famously in the 1997 movie Contact — but its real work is mapping the radio sky: supernova remnants, the jets of black holes, and the cosmic microwave background. Its railway tracks let the dishes be reconfigured into different arrangements.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the Very Large Array combines many dishes, then explain what interferometry achieves.

name: The Keck Telescopes
teaser: The Keck Observatory is a pair of twin telescopes atop Mauna Kea, each with a 10-meter mirror - among the largest in the world. Their secret is segmented mirrors: each primary is made of 36 hexagonal segments that work together as one, a pioneering design now used by many giant telescopes. The Keck telescopes have been powerhouses of discovery since the 1990s, from finding the first planets around other stars to probing the faintest galaxies in the early universe. With adaptive optics, they correct atmospheric blur and deliver images sharper than any telescope before them. California's twin giants are among the most scientifically productive instruments ever built.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why Keck's segmented mirrors are revolutionary, then explain why Mauna Kea is an ideal observing site.

name: The Chandra X-ray Observatory
teaser: The Chandra X-ray Observatory has been staring at the universe in X-rays since 1999, revealing the violent, hot, and energetic side of the cosmos that optical telescopes cannot see. X-rays come from the most extreme places: the swirling gas around black holes, the shockwaves of supernovae, and the million-degree gas in galaxy clusters. Chandra has imaged the remnants of exploded stars, spotted black holes devouring matter, and helped measure the dark matter holding galaxy clusters together. It operates from a highly elliptical orbit, far above Earth's absorbing atmosphere. Over two decades, its sharp X-ray eyes have transformed our picture of the universe's most violent places.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what X-ray astronomy reveals about hot, violent places, then explain why Chandra must sit above the atmosphere.

name: The Spitzer Space Telescope
teaser: The Spitzer Space Telescope was the last of NASA's four Great Observatories, and it saw the universe in infrared - the light of cool objects, dust, and distant galaxies. Launched in 2003, it trailed Earth in orbit, using liquid helium to cool its instruments to near absolute zero so its own heat would not blind them. After the helium ran out in 2009, engineers kept two cameras working in a 'warm mission' that ran for another decade. Spitzer revealed dusty planet-forming disks, the hidden nurseries of stars, and even measured the atmospheres of exoplanets. It was retired in 2020, its mission passed to its infrared successor, the James Webb Space Telescope.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Spitzer saw cool dust and exoplanets in infrared, then explain why its cooling ran out and it retired.

name: Why Observatories Sit on Mountains
teaser: The world's great observatories cluster in a handful of special places: high, dry, dark and stable. Mauna Kea in Hawaii stands 4,200 metres above the clouds, with some of the best 'seeing' on Earth. The Atacama Desert in Chile is the driest place on the planet — perfect for infrared and millimetre telescopes like ALMA. Remote sites like the Canary Islands, Hawaii and northern Chile offer dark skies far from city lights. Astronomers travel to these peaks because a telescope is only as good as the air above it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why astronomers build observatories on high mountains and in deserts, then explain how atmosphere and light pollution matter.

name: Adaptive Optics
teaser: Adaptive optics is the technology that lets telescopes beat the atmosphere's blur by correcting it in real time. A telescope with adaptive optics measures how the atmosphere is distorting starlight hundreds of times per second - using a guide star or laser - and flexes a small deformable mirror to cancel the distortion. The result: images as sharp as if the telescope were in space. The technology, first developed for military spy satellites and declassified in the 1990s, has transformed ground-based astronomy, letting Earth telescopes rival and sometimes exceed space observatories. Today, every major telescope uses adaptive optics to see planets, stars, and galaxies in breathtaking detail. The atmosphere's dance is now corrected with mirrors moving at light speed.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how adaptive optics removes atmospheric blur in real time, then explain how it made ground telescopes sharper.

name: Light Pollution
teaser: Light pollution is the glow that washes out the stars - wasted artificial light scattering through the atmosphere, brightening the sky and hiding all but the brightest objects. In cities, only a few dozen stars remain visible; in truly dark skies, thousands shine. Light pollution also disrupts wildlife, wastes energy, and has been linked to health effects. The problem is solvable: shielded fixtures that point light down, warmer bulbs, and sensible lighting design can cut the glow dramatically while improving safety. Dark sky parks and reserves around the world protect islands of darkness. Astronomy has given us a strong reason to care about lighting, and increasingly, cities are choosing to dim their glow and bring the stars back.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how artificial light washes out the night sky, then explain what dark-sky reserves do about it.

name: Astrophotography
teaser: Astrophotography turns telescopes and cameras into time machines, revealing detail no eye can see. A modern camera can capture the red glow of a nebula in a minute; stack 50 images and the faintest structures emerge. Techniques range from simple smartphone shots of the Moon to deep-sky imaging with computer-guided mounts and filters. The key is patience: exposures of hours, processed carefully, can bring out the colours of gas clouds that appear grey to the eye. Every astrophotographer is chasing the same thing — light that left its source long ago.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how astrophotography works and what it takes to photograph the night sky, then explain why long exposures matter.

name: Naked-Eye Astronomy
teaser: Before telescopes, humans knew the sky intimately with the naked eye alone - and you can too. The brightest stars, the wanderers we now call planets, the Milky Way, and occasional comets and meteors were all catalogued and named by careful observers. The naked eye can see about 6,000 stars from a dark site, the phases of the Moon, the Pleiades and other clusters, the Andromeda Galaxy as a faint smudge, and even a few nebulae. Our ancestors tracked the Sun and Moon precisely enough to predict eclipses and build calendars. Modern naked-eye astronomy is still rewarding: learn the constellations, watch the planets move, and the sky becomes a familiar, changing landscape. No equipment needed - just your eyes and a dark night.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what constellations, planets and satellites you can spot with no equipment, then explain how dark skies transform the view.

name: Planetariums
teaser: A planetarium is a theatre where the night sky is projected onto a dome, bringing the stars indoors. The first modern planetarium projector was built in 1923 by the Zeiss company in Germany, using a single machine with lenses for every star. Today's digital planetariums can fly you through the solar system, back to the Big Bang, or out to the edge of the observable universe. For millions of schoolchildren, the planetarium dome was their first voyage into space — and for many, the start of a lifelong obsession.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how planetariums project the sky and why they remain valuable, then explain how they help teach astronomy.

name: Amateur Astronomy
teaser: Amateur astronomy is the world's most popular science, practiced by millions of backyard observers who range from casual skywatchers to serious researchers. With binoculars, telescopes, and cameras, amateurs discover comets and supernovae, track asteroids, time occultations, and monitor variable stars - genuinely useful science that professionals welcome. They also simply enjoy the sky: learning constellations, watching meteor showers, and photographing the Moon and planets. Amateur astronomy is famously welcoming and free, needing nothing but clear skies to begin. From Galileo - the first amateur astronomer - to today's smartphone-connected telescopes, the hobby has always been where the love of the cosmos begins. You do not need a degree to explore the universe; you just need to look up.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how amateur astronomers contribute real discoveries, then explain what equipment you actually need to start.

name: Nicolaus Copernicus
teaser: Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish canon and astronomer, overturned 1,500 years of thought. In 1543 he published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, arguing that the Sun — not Earth — sits at the centre, with Earth spinning daily and orbiting the Sun yearly. His heliocentric model was far simpler than the old Earth-centred system with its epicycles, but it was revolutionary and risky. Copernicus was careful: he only published as he lay dying. His book lit the fuse of the Scientific Revolution, even though his own model still used circular orbits.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Copernicus placed the Sun at the center and why he delayed publishing, then explain what the heliocentric model changed.

name: Galileo Galilei
teaser: Galileo Galilei turned a new invention — the telescope — to the heavens in 1609 and changed everything. He saw mountains on the Moon, discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter (proving not everything circles Earth), and watched Venus show phases that only made sense if it orbited the Sun. He also observed sunspots and the Milky Way's countless stars. His defence of the Copernican model brought him before the Inquisition in 1633, forcing him to recant under threat of torture. He died under house arrest — yet his telescopes opened the modern cosmos.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Galileo's observations of moons, phases and sunspots, then explain why they put him in conflict with the Church.

name: Johannes Kepler
teaser: Johannes Kepler was the mathematician who cracked planetary motion. Using Tycho Brahe's superb observations of Mars, he spent years computing and found the orbits were ellipses, not circles — his first law, published in 1609. His three laws describe how planets speed up near the Sun and how their orbital periods relate to distance. Kepler's laws turned astronomy into a predictive science and directly prepared the ground for Newton's theory of gravity. Kepler also studied optics, and his name now graces a planet-hunting space telescope that found thousands of worlds.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn Kepler's three laws of planetary motion, then explain how he found them from data with no telescopes.

name: Tycho Brahe
teaser: Tycho Brahe was the last great astronomer to work without a telescope — and one of the most flamboyant. A Danish nobleman with a brass nose after a duel, he built an island observatory, Uraniborg, where he spent 20 years measuring star and planet positions with unprecedented accuracy, using giant instruments and pure patience. His catalogue of 777 stars was the best of its era, and his meticulous Mars data — passed to his assistant Kepler — made possible the discovery of elliptical orbits. Brahe also stunned Europe with his 1572 supernova observation, proving the heavens could change.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Tycho Brahe's precise observations paved the way for Kepler, then explain why his measurements were so accurate.

name: Isaac Newton and Gravity
teaser: Isaac Newton unified the heavens and the Earth with a single idea: universal gravitation. In 1687's Principia, he showed that the same force that makes an apple fall also keeps the Moon in orbit and planets circling the Sun. His law of gravity, combined with his three laws of motion and his new mathematics of calculus, let astronomers predict eclipses, comets and planetary motions with stunning precision. Newton also built the first practical reflecting telescope and studied light and colour. He is often called the greatest scientist who ever lived.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Newton's law of universal gravitation explained the motions Kepler described, then explain how it still guides spaceflight.

name: Edmond Halley
teaser: Edmond Halley was the first person to realize a comet could return. In 1682 he observed a bright comet and, using Newton's new theory of gravity, calculated that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were the same object — returning about every 76 years. He predicted its return in 1758; when it appeared on schedule, long after his death, it was named Halley's Comet. Halley also mapped the southern sky, studied magnetism and helped fund Newton's Principia. He was the man who proved comets are citizens, not omens.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Halley predicted his comet's return using Newton's math, then explain why the prediction was a landmark.

name: William Herschel
teaser: William Herschel was a German-born musician who became the greatest observer of his age — and accidentally discovered a planet. In 1781, while sweeping the sky with his homemade telescope, he spotted an object that moved against the stars: Uranus, the first planet found since antiquity. George III appointed him King's Astronomer, and Herschel built ever-larger telescopes, mapping the Milky Way, discovering infrared radiation and cataloguing thousands of nebulae. His sister Caroline worked alongside him, discovering eight comets and helping with his catalogues.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Herschel found Uranus by accident, then explain his other discoveries from infrared light to double stars.

name: Caroline Herschel
teaser: Caroline Herschel was the first professional woman astronomer — paid for her work, in 1787, as assistant to her brother William. She discovered eight comets, including one in 1786 that made her famous, and compiled a catalogue of 2,500 nebulae that remained standard for a century. Born in Hanover, she worked without pay for years, recording her brother's observations in her spare hours. The Royal Astronomical Society awarded her its Gold Medal in 1828 — an honour not given to another woman for 168 years.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Caroline Herschel's comet discoveries and her work helping her brother, then explain why she became the first paid female astronomer.

name: Henrietta Leavitt
teaser: Henrietta Swan Leavitt made one of the most important discoveries in astronomy from a desk at Harvard, where she studied photographic plates as one of the 'Harvard Computers'. She noticed that brighter Cepheid variable stars pulsate more slowly — a precise relationship between brightness and period. That gave astronomers a cosmic ruler: measure a Cepheid's period, and you know its true brightness; compare with how dim it appears, and you know its distance. Her 1912 discovery let Hubble measure the universe's scale and expansion, though she never knew it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Leavitt's study of variable stars let astronomers measure the universe, then explain what a Cepheid variable is.

name: Edwin Hubble
teaser: Edwin Hubble was the man who discovered the universe is far bigger — and younger — than anyone imagined. In 1924, using the 100-inch Mount Wilson telescope, he proved that 'Andromeda' was a galaxy far beyond the Milky Way, expanding the cosmos a millionfold. Then, measuring distances to galaxies with Henrietta Leavitt's Cepheid method, he found the farther they were, the faster they fled — the expanding universe, announced in 1929. Hubble's law became the foundation of Big Bang cosmology, and his name now rides a space telescope.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Hubble's discovery that galaxies are fleeing from us, then explain how his work changed our picture of the cosmos.

name: Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin
teaser: Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin was the astronomer who discovered what stars are made of. In her 1925 doctoral thesis at Harvard — the first PhD in astronomy awarded to a woman at that university — she showed that stars are almost entirely hydrogen and helium, not iron like Earth. The idea was so shocking that her advisor urged her to soften the conclusion. Decades later she was proved completely right. She went on to study variable stars and teach at Harvard, and is now recognized as one of the most important astronomers of the 20th century.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Cecilia Payne discovered that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium, then explain why her thesis was initially dismissed.

name: Vera Rubin
teaser: Vera Rubin never set out to find dark matter — she set out to measure how galaxies spin. In the 1970s, working with Kent Ford, she measured the rotation speeds of stars across whole galaxies and found something impossible: stars at the edges orbit just as fast as stars near the centre, even though there isn't enough visible mass to hold them. The only explanation: invisible matter surrounding the galaxies. Her careful measurements convinced astronomers that dark matter exists and outweighs the visible universe. She was denied the Nobel, but her discovery reshaped cosmology.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Rubin's galaxy rotation measurements revealed dark matter, then explain the evidence she gathered.

name: Carl Sagan
teaser: Carl Sagan was the astronomer who brought the universe to the world. A planetary scientist at Cornell, he helped design the messages on the Voyager Golden Records and advised NASA missions to Mars. But his greatest legacy is communication: his 1980 television series Cosmos reached 400 million viewers, and his line 'we are made of star-stuff' became iconic. His 1994 book Pale Blue Dot — inspired by a Voyager photo of Earth as a mote of light — is among the most quoted science writing ever. Sagan died in 1996, but Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey and the search for life he championed continue.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Carl Sagan made science accessible and explored the possibility of life, then explain his role in planetary missions.

name: Stephen Hawking
teaser: Stephen Hawking spent his life at the meeting point of gravity, black holes and the quantum world. Confined to a wheelchair by ALS, he used his mind to show, in 1974, that black holes are not truly black — they leak radiation and slowly evaporate, a result combining general relativity and quantum mechanics that stunned physics. His 1988 bestseller A Brief History of Time sold 10 million copies despite famously containing 'only one equation'. He also argued the universe needs no creator. His name will forever be linked with black holes and the big questions.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Hawking's work on black holes and his famous radiation, then explain what Hawking radiation actually is.

name: Tycho's Supernova
teaser: In November 1572, a 'new star' blazed in the constellation Cassiopeia, bright enough to see in daylight. Tycho Brahe — then a young Danish nobleman — observed it obsessively and proved it was far beyond the Moon, because it showed no parallax as Earth moved. That demolished the ancient belief that the heavens were perfect and unchanging. We now know the 'new star' was a supernova, the explosion of a white dwarf, whose remnant still glows in X-rays today. It's called SN 1572, or simply Tycho's Supernova.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the 1572 supernova challenged the idea of an unchanging sky, then explain what its remnant shows today.

name: Harlow Shapley
teaser: Harlow Shapley was the astronomer who mapped our place in the galaxy. In 1917, using the positions of globular clusters — dense balls of stars that orbit the galactic centre — he showed the Sun is not at the Milky Way's centre but far out in the disk, about two-thirds of the way to the edge. It was a Copernican blow to human vanity on a cosmic scale. Shapley then became director of Harvard Observatory, where he famously debated Heber Curtis over whether 'spiral nebulae' were other galaxies — a debate Hubble settled.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Shapley used globular clusters to locate the Milky Way's center, then explain how the picture changed again.

name: Early Planet Hunters
teaser: William Lassell and William Cranch Bond were 19th-century telescope pioneers. Lassell, a wealthy English brewer, ground large mirrors himself and used them to discover Triton, Neptune's largest moon, in 1846, and two moons of Uranus — Ariel and Umbriel. Bond, first director of the Harvard Observatory, took the first photograph of a star in 1850 and helped capture the first photo of the Moon. Both men pushed the art of telescope-making and opened the solar system's dimmer corners to view.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how 19th-century astronomers found moons of Neptune and Saturn, then explain why their giant telescopes mattered.

name: Observing Mars: Then and Now
teaser: Mars has been studied since the first telescopes, and the story of its mapping is a story of growing understanding. Giovanni Schiaparelli drew 'canali' — channels — in 1877, which Percival Lowell sensationalized as canals built by a dying civilization. Spacecraft finally settled the matter: the canals were optical illusions and the 'waves of darkening' were dust storms. From Herschel's drawings to Mariner 4's first flyby photos in 1965, every generation improved the picture. Today rovers photograph the surface in colour, but the old drawings remain a beautiful reminder of how little we knew.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how early drawings of Mars gave way to spacecraft images, then explain how our view of the planet has changed.

name: Jocelyn Bell Burnell
teaser: In 1967, graduate student Jocelyn Bell Burnell was scanning radio data for quasars when she noticed a puzzling signal — pulses every 1.3 seconds, so regular she nicknamed the source 'LGM-1' for Little Green Men. It was the first pulsar, a spinning neutron star sweeping a beam of radio light past Earth. The discovery won the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics — awarded to her supervisor, not to Bell, a slight that became a famous case study in scientific credit. She went on to a distinguished career and later used her award money to fund students from underrepresented groups.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Jocelyn Bell discovered the first pulsar and why her advisor got the Nobel Prize, then explain what pulsars are.

name: The Golden Record
teaser: The Voyager Golden Records are humanity's message in a bottle — two gold-plated copper phonograph records launched in 1977 aboard Voyager 1 and 2, designed to outlast us and explain us to any civilization that finds them. Each record holds 116 images, greetings in 55 languages, natural sounds (whales, wind, thunder), music from Bach to Chuck Berry, and an encoded message from President Carter. The cover diagrams explain how to play the record and locate Earth. Carl Sagan chaired the selection committee. The records will travel for billions of years, the most enduring artifacts we've ever made — Earth's self-portrait, sailing the galaxy.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what the Voyager Golden Records contain and why they were sent, then explain how a future finder could decode them.

name: Sputnik
teaser: Sputnik 2, launched a month after Sputnik 1 in November 1957, carried the first living creature into orbit — the dog Laika. It was a propaganda masterstroke: a half-tonne satellite with a dog aboard proved the Soviets' rockets could carry something substantial, and it foreshadowed human spaceflight. But the mission had no recovery plan; Laika died in orbit, a fact the Soviets hid until the 1970s. The flight's moral cost sparked debate about animal testing and weighed on the program for decades. Sputnik 2 burned up in the atmosphere in April 1958. It was a triumph of engineering and a tragedy of ethics, tangled together.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Sputnik became the first artificial satellite and why it shocked the world, then explain what its beeping signal proved.

name: Laika: The First Traveler
teaser: In November 1957, a stray Moscow dog named Laika became the first living creature to orbit Earth, aboard Sputnik 2. She was chosen for her calm temperament, and the mission was a propaganda triumph for the Soviets. But there was no re-entry plan: Laika died in orbit, probably within hours from stress and heat, a fact the USSR concealed for decades. Her flight proved a living being could survive launch and weightlessness — and it sparked decades of debate about animal testing in space. A monument in Moscow honours her.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the story of Laika and what her flight taught scientists, then explain why her mission could not bring her home.

name: Yuri Gagarin
teaser: On April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once in his Vostok 1 capsule in just 108 minutes. The 27-year-old Soviet pilot's calm radio call — 'Poyekhali!' ('Let's go!') — became legendary, and his return, parachuting out of his capsule after re-entry, made him the most famous man on Earth. His flight proved humans could survive space travel, kicking the Space Race into high gear. Gagarin died in a 1968 jet crash and became a hero forever: April 12 is now Cosmonautics Day worldwide.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Gagarin's historic 108-minute orbit and why he became a global hero, then explain what his flight proved.

name: Valentina Tereshkova
teaser: Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space on June 16, 1963, piloting Vostok 6 — flying solo for nearly three days and completing 48 orbits. She was a textile worker and amateur parachutist recruited into the cosmonaut corps, and her flight remains the only time a woman has flown in space alone. The flight was gruelling — she was sick for much of it — but she completed her mission. The Soviets waited 19 years to fly another woman in space, and Tereshkova went on to a long political career.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Tereshkova flew alone in orbit and how the space programs treated women, then explain the gap before the next woman flew.

name: Apollo 11
teaser: Apollo 11 was the mission that fulfilled humanity's oldest dream. On July 16, 1969, the Saturn V lifted off from Cape Kennedy with Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins aboard. Four days later, the lunar module Eagle descended to the Sea of Tranquility with just 25 seconds of fuel to spare, and Armstrong's boot touched the dust at 02:56 UTC on July 21. The crew spent 21 hours on the surface, collecting 21.5 kg of samples, planting a flag, and leaving a plaque: 'We came in peace for all mankind.' They returned to a world of celebration — an estimated 600 million people had watched. It was one small step, and it was ours.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Apollo 11 landed humans on the Moon and what the astronauts did there, then explain what the mission returned to Earth.

name: Neil Armstrong
teaser: Neil Armstrong was the first person to set foot on another world. A naval aviator who flew in the Korean War and test-flew the X-15 rocket plane, he joined NASA in 1962. On July 20, 1969, he manually piloted the lunar module Eagle past boulders to a safe landing with only seconds of fuel to spare, then stepped onto the Moon. Famously private, Armstrong largely withdrew from public life, teaching engineering and serving on commissions. His quiet words and his courage defined an age.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Armstrong's career from test pilot to Moonwalker, then explain why his famous first words were chosen carefully.

name: Voyager 1
teaser: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the farthest human-made object from Earth — over 24 billion kilometres away as of the 2020s, and still speeding outward. It flew past Jupiter and Saturn, photographing their moons for the first time, and in 2012 became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. In 1990 it turned back and captured the Pale Blue Dot — Earth as a single pixel of light. It carries a Golden Record, and its plutonium power will keep it talking until about 2025. Its messages take more than 20 hours to reach us.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Voyager 1's grand tour and its entry into interstellar space, then explain what it found at the edge of the solar system.

name: Voyager 2
teaser: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited all four giant planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — completing the 'Grand Tour' that the planets' rare alignment made possible. Launched in 1977, it revealed Uranus's sideways world and Neptune's violent storms, discovered 11 new moons, and is the only probe to have flown past Neptune, in 1989. It then became the second spacecraft to reach interstellar space, in 2018. Its instruments still report back from beyond the heliosphere, and its 1977 launch-era computers are a marvel of endurance engineering.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Voyager 2 visited Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, then explain what makes its flybys unique.

name: Launching Hubble
teaser: The Hubble Space Telescope nearly died at birth. Launched aboard Discovery in April 1990, it immediately sent back images so blurred that scientists called it 'Hubble Trouble' — the main mirror had been ground to the wrong shape. The flaw was tiny, just 2.2 microns, but catastrophic. Rather than abandon it, NASA planned one of the riskiest missions in history: a shuttle crew would install corrective optics in 1993. The repair worked perfectly, and within months Hubble was delivering the razor-sharp images that made it famous. The launch's failure became its greatest triumph.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Hubble's launch and early troubles, then explain how astronauts serviced it across five missions.

name: The International Space Station
teaser: The International Space Station is the largest structure ever built in space and humanity's most ambitious engineering project: a football-field-sized laboratory orbiting 400 kilometers above Earth. Built and operated by 15 nations, it has been continuously inhabited since November 2000 - meaning humans have lived in space every single day of the 21st century. Crews conduct thousands of experiments in biology, physics, and medicine that can only be done in weightlessness. The ISS is also a remarkable act of international cooperation, assembled in orbit by astronauts and cosmonauts who once belonged to rival space programs. It is the modern world's greatest shared achievement in orbit.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the ISS was assembled piece by piece and why it orbits at 400 kilometers, then explain how crews live there.

name: Curiosity on Mars
teaser: NASA's Curiosity rover landed on Mars in August 2012 using a daring 'sky crane' that lowered it on cables. The car-sized, nuclear-powered rover has since climbed Mount Sharp, a mountain in Gale Crater, drilling rocks and discovering that Mars was once warm and wet enough to host lakes — and possibly life. Its instruments have found organic molecules, methane in the air, and evidence that conditions were habitable for long stretches. Curiosity was designed for a 2-year mission and has explored for over a decade, rolling farther and climbing higher than any rover before it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Curiosity landed with its sky crane and what it discovered, then explain why it studies rocks and weather.

name: Perseverance and Ingenuity
teaser: Perseverance, NASA's most advanced rover, landed in Mars's Jezero Crater in February 2021 on a mission to search for signs of ancient life. Jezero once held a lake and river delta — prime real estate for fossil hunting — and the rover is drilling and caching rock cores for a future return-to-Earth mission. It also carried Ingenuity, the first helicopter to fly on another world, which made 72 flights before a 2024 crash. Perseverance is a robot geologist, astrobiologist and engineer all in one, writing Mars's history one sample at a time.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Perseverance's mission to cache Mars samples and Ingenuity's first helicopter flights, then explain what the samples may tell us.

name: New Horizons
teaser: New Horizons is the spacecraft that made Pluto a real world. Launched in January 2006 — the fastest spacecraft ever to leave Earth — it flew past Pluto in July 2015 after a nine-and-a-half-year journey, returning images that transformed the dwarf planet from a blurry dot into a landscape of ice mountains, nitrogen plains and a heart-shaped glacier. It then flew past Arrokoth, the most distant object ever visited, in January 2019, revealing a pristine snowman-shaped relic of the solar system's birth. New Horizons continues outward through the Kuiper Belt, healthy and exploring. It carries the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, who discovered Pluto in 1930 — the first explorer to be buried on a journey to the world he found.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about New Horizons' flyby of Pluto and the Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth, then explain why the journey took nearly ten years.

name: Juno at Jupiter
teaser: Juno is a NASA orbiter that has been diving close to Jupiter since 2016, on a mission to understand the giant planet from the inside out. It measures the magnetic field, maps the gravity field and peers beneath the clouds with microwave radiometry, finding that Jupiter's interior is far more complex than expected. Juno is solar-powered, with three giant panels the size of basketball courts, and its highly elliptical orbit threads it between Jupiter and its radiation belts. It has also photographed the planet's auroras and storms in stunning detail.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Juno's orbit over Jupiter's poles and what it found, then explain why the mission will end in the atmosphere.

name: Cassini and Huygens
teaser: Cassini was NASA's magnificent mission to Saturn — thirteen years in orbit, from 2004 to 2017, studying the ringed planet, its rings and its moons. It discovered geysers on Enceladus, the liquid methane lakes of Titan, and sent the Huygens probe to land on Titan's surface — the most distant landing ever attempted. Cassini photographed the rings at incredible resolution and watched seasons change on Saturn. In 2017, running low on fuel, it was deliberately plunged into Saturn's atmosphere, ending its mission in a fiery dive while protecting the moons it had studied.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Cassini studied Saturn and its moons and dropped the Huygens probe on Titan, then explain why it ended in a deliberate plunge.

name: Parker Solar Probe
teaser: The Parker Solar Probe is the fastest spacecraft ever built and the closest any human-made object has come to the Sun. Launched in 2018, it repeatedly dives through the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, protected by a carbon heat shield that endures temperatures of 1,400 degrees Celsius. On each close pass, Parker samples the solar wind, magnetic fields, and plasma right where they are born, flying at speeds above 600,000 kilometers per hour. It has already revealed mysteries of the corona's heat and the wind's acceleration. Named after Eugene Parker, the physicist who predicted the solar wind, the probe is touching the Sun to understand it.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Parker Solar Probe flies through the Sun's corona, then explain why it must travel faster than anything before.

name: Artemis: Back to the Moon
teaser: Artemis is NASA's program to return humans to the Moon — named for Apollo's twin sister, a fitting successor to the Apollo program. The plan: the Orion capsule, launched by the giant SLS rocket, carries crews to a small station called Gateway in lunar orbit, then down to the surface, including the first woman and first person of colour. Artemis I flew an uncrewed loop around the Moon in 2022. The goal is a sustainable lunar presence — and a proving ground for the longer journey to Mars. The Moon is once again the frontier.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Artemis program and its goal to return humans to the Moon, then explain how it will lead to Mars.

name: Starship
teaser: Starship is SpaceX's ambitious plan for a fully reusable spacecraft system - a giant stainless steel rocket designed to carry crew and cargo to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Standing about 120 meters tall, it combines the Super Heavy booster and the Starship spacecraft, both designed to land and fly again like airplanes. Its Raptor engines burn methane, which could someday be manufactured on Mars. Starship is the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, and SpaceX has been testing it with increasingly ambitious flights, catching the booster with giant mechanical arms. If it succeeds, Starship could make space travel dramatically cheaper - and make Mars colonization conceivable.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Starship is designed to be fully reusable, then explain the role it is meant to play in deep space travel.

name: Building the ISS
teaser: The International Space Station is a jigsaw puzzle of modules assembled in orbit. The first piece, Russia's Zarya, launched in 1998, followed by the US Unity node and a parade of modules: Zvezda, Destiny, Columbus, Kibo, Harmony, Tranquility and more, each built by a different nation and launched by different rockets. Astronauts connected them with robotic arms and spacewalks over two decades. The station is a flying demonstration that international cooperation works even at the edge of space — and its modules are all still sealing and functioning after 25 years in orbit.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the ISS was assembled module by module, then explain why international cooperation was essential.

name: Reentry: Coming Home
teaser: Re-entering Earth's atmosphere is one of the most dangerous moments in spaceflight. A spacecraft returning from orbit slams into the air at about 28,000 km/h, and friction and compression heat the atmosphere around it to thousands of degrees — hotter than the Sun's surface. The key is the heat shield, which absorbs the fury while the vehicle decelerates from orbital speed to a parachute landing in minutes. Apollo capsules, the Space Shuttle's tiles and SpaceX's Dragon all survive this trial. Get the angle wrong and you skip off the atmosphere like a stone on water — or burn up entirely.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why reentry heats spacecraft to thousands of degrees, then explain how heat shields and parachutes bring crews home.

name: How Astronauts Train
teaser: Becoming an astronaut takes years of preparation for moments that last minutes. Candidates train in simulators for every mission phase, fly parabolic aircraft to feel weightlessness, and practise spacewalks in a giant swimming pool called the Neutral Buoyancy Lab, rehearsing every move for six hours underwater for every hour in space. They learn Russian, medicine, geology and robotics, and they train to survive wilderness and water landings. The selection itself is famously brutal: of tens of thousands of applicants, NASA picks a handful every few years. The training is a marathon, and the payoff is a few days in space.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how astronauts train in simulators, pools and aircraft, then explain why emergency drills take so much time.

name: Spacesuits
teaser: A spacesuit is a personal spacecraft — a pressurized shell providing oxygen, temperature control, water, power and protection from vacuum and radiation. The suit used for spacewalks is a two-piece pressure garment with a backpack life-support system, and it can keep an astronaut alive for up to eight hours. It's heavy — about 130 kg on Earth, weightless in orbit — and surprisingly stiff, so astronauts train extensively to move in it. The gloves are the hardest part to master. Every suit is tailored, and every one is a miracle of engineering that stands between its wearer and death.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how spacesuits protect astronauts from vacuum and extremes, then explain how they supply air, water and cooling.

name: Spacewalks
teaser: Spacewalks - officially called extravehicular activities, or EVAs - are the most physically demanding and exhilarating work an astronaut can do. Wearing a spacesuit that is essentially a tiny spacecraft, an astronaut floats outside the station to install equipment, repair hardware, or perform experiments. The first spacewalk was Alexei Leonov's in 1965; since then, thousands have been performed. Spacewalkers work in pairs, tethered and guided by careful checklists, with a full day of prep beforehand. Each walk lasts five to eight hours and leaves the astronaut exhausted but euphoric. Looking down at Earth from outside your spaceship is, by all accounts, the greatest view in the universe.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what it takes to spacewalk and why astronauts practice underwater, then explain the dangers of a suit failure.

name: Sleeping in Space
teaser: In space, there is no up or down, so sleeping is wherever you anchor yourself. Astronauts on the ISS sleep in small personal cabins, strapped into sleeping bags that float if released. There is no pillow - your head just drifts - and no need to lie flat, since gravity is not pulling blood anywhere. Many astronauts report floating in their sleep with their arms drifting outward, the classic 'weightless sleeper' pose. The space station orbits Earth every 90 minutes, so crews see a sunrise and sunset every 45 minutes, and most use an eye mask to simulate night. Surprisingly, many astronauts sleep better in space than on Earth, away from phones and traffic noise.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why astronauts sleep in sleeping bags attached to walls, then explain the sunrise-every-90-minutes problem.

name: Eating in Space
teaser: Space food has evolved from tubes of paste to fresh tortillas. Early astronauts squeezed pureed beef and applesauce from aluminium tubes; by the Apollo era, bite-sized cubes and freeze-dried packets were standard. Today the ISS menu includes shrimp cocktail, beef stroganoff, thermostabilized tacos and even fresh fruit and vegetables delivered by resupply ships. Astronauts also grow lettuce and radishes on board. There's no fridge and no gravity, so food is stabilized, rehydrated or eaten quickly — and tortillas beat bread because crumbs would float into eyes and equipment.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how space food has changed from pastes to real meals, then explain why taste and crumbs are tricky in orbit.

name: Life Without Gravity
teaser: Weightlessness is hard on the human body. Fluids shift toward the head, giving astronauts puffy faces and skinny legs; bones lose calcium, muscles weaken, and spines stretch — crew members return several centimetres taller. Eyesight can blur, balance systems scramble, and astronauts exercise two hours a day to fight the decay. Most effects reverse after returning to Earth, but some, like vision changes and bone loss, may linger. That's why long-duration spaceflight, like a future Mars mission, remains one of medicine's greatest challenges — and why the ISS is our laboratory for understanding it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how microgravity affects muscles, bones and fluids, then explain what astronauts do to stay healthy.

name: Sally Ride
teaser: Sally Ride became the first American woman in space on June 18, 1983, aboard the shuttle Challenger. A physicist and former tennis player, she was one of six women selected in NASA's first class of female astronauts in 1978. On her second flight in 1984, she used the shuttle's robotic arm — which she had helped design — to capture a satellite in orbit. After Challenger's 1986 disaster, she served on the investigation panel and spent the rest of her career teaching and inspiring girls in science. America honoured her with a stamp, and her legacy lives on in thousands of young scientists.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Sally Ride's historic flight and her later work teaching science, then explain why her mission mattered.

name: Mae Jemison
teaser: Mae Jemison became the first Black woman in space on September 12, 1992, aboard the shuttle Endeavour. A physician who had served in the Peace Corps in Sierra Leone and Liberia, she trained as a dancer and studied chemical engineering before joining NASA in 1987. During her eight-day mission she conducted experiments on bone cells and weightlessness. She famously opened her flights with the phrase 'Habari Gani?' — a Swahili greeting. After leaving NASA she founded a technology company and championed science education, saying she wanted to see 'a million more girls in space'.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Mae Jemison's journey from doctor to astronaut, then explain how her science mission benefited research.

name: Chris Hadfield
teaser: Chris Hadfield made space feel human to millions. The Canadian astronaut commanded the ISS in 2013 and became a global sensation by recording a music video of David Bowie's Space Oddity aboard the station — the first music video made in space. He also posted photos, answered questions and showed how astronauts brush their teeth and cry in space, demystifying life in orbit. Hadfield flew three missions, performed two spacewalks and served as the first Canadian to command the station. After retiring, he wrote bestsellers and inspired a generation to look up.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Chris Hadfield used music and social media to share space life, then explain what he taught millions about orbit.

name: Women in Spaceflight
teaser: The women who flew to space in the early era — Valentina Tereshkova, Svetlana Savitskaya, Sally Ride and others — broke the final frontier's glass ceiling one flight at a time. Savitskaya was the first woman to walk in space in 1984, and Helen Sharman became the first British astronaut in 1991. Today women are regular crew members, commanders and spacewalkers on the ISS, and NASA's Artemis program is planning the first woman on the Moon. Their progress mirrors a broader truth: space was built by humanity, and it.

exploreAction.instruction: Explore the history of women in space from Tereshkova to today, then explain how the astronaut corps changed over time.

name: The First Exoplanets
teaser: Before 1995, we didn't know for certain that planets exist beyond our solar system. That year, astronomers found the first planet around a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b — a 'hot Jupiter' closer to its star than Mercury is to our Sun. The discovery opened a floodgate: we now know of more than 5,000 confirmed exoplanets, and the count keeps climbing. They range from scorching gas giants to rocky 'super-Earths' in habitable zones. The galaxy, it turns out, is teeming with planets — our solar system is just one family among countless others.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the first exoplanet was found in 1995, then explain why finding planets around sunlike stars took so long.

name: The Transit Method
teaser: The transit method finds planets by watching for tiny eclipses. When a planet passes in front of its star, it blocks a sliver of starlight — typically less than one percent — and the star dims measurably. The dip's size reveals the planet's size, and the time between dips reveals its orbit. NASA's Kepler telescope used transits to find thousands of planets by staring at one patch of sky, and TESS now scans the whole sky the same way. It's the most successful planet-hunting technique ever devised — a blink-and-you'll-miss-it shadow hunt.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the transit method works and why it is so productive, then explain what the dimming reveals about a planet.

name: The Wobble Method
teaser: The radial velocity method finds planets by watching a star wobble. A planet's gravity tugs on its star, pulling it slightly toward and away from us, shifting the star's light by a tiny amount each orbit — the Doppler effect, like a siren's pitch change. The wobble reveals the planet's minimum mass and orbital period. This technique found the first exoplanets in the 1990s and measures them independently of the transit method. It's slower and needs enormous patience, but it works for stars in any orientation and catches planets at any angle.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how astronomers detect planets by watching a star wobble, then explain what the wobble size tells them.

name: The Kepler Mission
teaser: NASA's Kepler mission, launched in 2009, stared at one patch of sky in the constellation Cygnus for four years, watching 150,000 stars for the telltale dips of transiting planets. The results were historic: over 2,600 confirmed planets, including many 'super-Earths' and the first rocky worlds in habitable zones. Kepler proved that planets are more common than stars themselves — and that small, rocky worlds like Earth are abundant. When the mission ended in 2018, it had rewritten the story of our place in the galaxy: there are billions of Earth-sized worlds out there.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Kepler stared at one patch of sky and found thousands of planets, then explain what its data proved about planet frequency.

name: TESS: Planet Hunter
teaser: TESS — the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite — is NASA's planet hunter for our cosmic neighbourhood. Launched in 2018, it divides the sky into sectors and watches bright, nearby stars for the dips of transiting planets, covering the whole sky in about two years. Where Kepler found distant worlds, TESS finds planets around the stars closest to us — the ones we can study in detail and even photograph. It has already catalogued thousands of candidates and hundreds of confirmed worlds, including several in habitable zones. These nearby planets are the prime targets for the James Webb Space Telescope.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how TESS finds exoplanets around nearby stars, then explain how it complements Kepler's deep stare.

name: The Habitable Zone
teaser: The habitable zone, often called the Goldilocks zone, is the ring around a star where a planet's surface could have liquid water - not too hot to boil it away, not too cold to freeze it solid. Its distance depends on the star: a bright star's zone lies far out, a dim star's zone hugs close in. But the zone is only a rough guide - a planet's atmosphere, greenhouse gases, and geology can make a world habitable well outside it, as Venus and Mars demonstrate in our own solar system. The concept focuses the search for life on the most promising planets, even as astronomers keep discovering that the rules for habitability are more flexible than anyone expected.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what the habitable zone is and why it matters, then explain how a planet's atmosphere can move the goalposts.

name: TRAPPIST-1 and Its Seven Worlds
teaser: TRAPPIST-1 is a small, cool red dwarf star about 40 light-years away — and it hosts an extraordinary family: seven Earth-sized, rocky planets, all packed into orbits closer than Mercury's. Three of them sit in the habitable zone, and the system is so compact that its planets' gravitational pull on each other can be measured. It's the best laboratory we have for studying rocky worlds around other stars, and the James Webb Space Telescope has already probed the atmospheres of its innermost planets. This miniature solar system may be the best place to find life's first signs.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the TRAPPIST-1 system and why three of its seven planets interest astrobiologists, then explain what makes the system special.

name: Proxima Centauri b
teaser: Proxima b is the closest known exoplanet to Earth — just 4.2 light-years away, orbiting the red dwarf Proxima Centauri. Discovered in 2016, it's roughly Earth-sized and sits in the habitable zone, where liquid water could exist. But its star is a flare star that blasts the planet with radiation, and Proxima b is likely tidally locked, one side always facing its sun. Whether it could host life is an open question — and it's the most reachable target for a future interstellar mission. Its discoverers called it 'a first step into a new frontier'.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the planet orbiting our nearest star and the debate over its habitability, then explain why we still know so little about it.

name: Hot Jupiters
teaser: Hot Jupiters are giant planets that orbit scorchingly close to their stars, completing a year in just days. The first exoplanet found around a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, was a hot Jupiter, and it shocked astronomers - nothing like it exists in our solar system.
