Seismologists even use tidal stress to understand earthquake timing. The Moon is not just pulling the oceans; it's kneading the entire planet like a ball of dough.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the Moon pulls not just the sea but the solid ground, then explain how sensitive instruments measure the rise.

name: Earth as an Exoplanet
teaser: We can detect habitable planets from light-years away — and studying Earth from space is the rehearsal. By looking at Earth as if it were an exoplanet, scientists learn what 'Earth-like' looks like from afar: the spectral fingerprints of water, oxygen, ozone and methane in the atmosphere, the red edge of vegetation, the glint of oceans. NASA's DSCOVR satellite photographs the sunlit Earth from a million kilometres away, imaging our planet as a pale dot — exactly how an alien telescope would see us. The trick of studying our own world from space teaches us how to recognize life elsewhere. Earth is the only biosignature we know, and we're learning to read it.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how astronomers treat Earth as a reference for exoplanet observation, then explain what our atmosphere would look like from afar.

name: Earth vs Venus
teaser: Earth and Venus are near twins — similar size, mass and distance from the Sun — yet they went completely different ways. Venus, with its runaway greenhouse effect, became a 465-degree furnace with sulfuric acid clouds and crushing pressure; Earth stayed temperate, wet and alive. The difference likely came down to a few factors: Venus lost its water (or never had much), which robbed it of oceans and plate tectonics; a slow spin and thick CO2 atmosphere sealed its fate. The two worlds are the solar system's great experiment in planetary divergence — and Venus is the cautionary tale that shows how thin Earth's habitability line really is.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Earth and Venus started similar but became opposites, then explain what made their climates diverge.

name: Mariner 9
teaser: Mariner 9 made history in 1971 as the first spacecraft to orbit another planet. It arrived at Mars just in time for a planet-wide dust storm, waited months for the dust to clear, then revealed a world beyond imagination: volcanoes taller than Everest, a canyon system dwarfing the Grand Canyon, dry riverbeds and a surface scarred by billions of years of history. Mariner 9 photographed 85 percent of Mars and mapped it at better resolution than anyone had seen. Its images ended the fantasy of canals and begun the real science of Mars — and its maps were used to pick the landing sites for the Vikings.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Mariner 9 reached Mars before the Moon landings ended and mapped the planet, then explain why it was a first.

name: The Viking Landers
teaser: The Viking landers were the first spacecraft to touch the surface of Mars — and the first to search for life there. In 1976, Viking 1 and 2 landed on opposite sides of the red planet and ran a suite of experiments, including three designed to test for living microbes. The results were famously ambiguous: one experiment showed chemistry consistent with life, others contradicted it, and most scientists concluded the activity was chemical, not biological. The Viking missions were a watershed: they delivered the first surface images, weather reports and the verdict that Mars's surface chemistry is fascinating but probably lifeless. Half a century later, the search for Mars life continues with better tools.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the Viking landers tested Martian soil for life in 1976, then explain why the results are still debated.

name: Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner
teaser: Pathfinder was the little mission that changed Mars exploration. Launched in 1996 and landed in 1997 using airbags that bounced across the surface, it deployed Sojourner — the first rover to roll on another planet. Sojourner was the size of a microwave oven, drove just 100 metres, and captured the public imagination with its photographs of the rocky Ares Vallis floodplain. Pathfinder proved that cheap, fast 'better, faster, cheaper' missions could reach Mars — and it opened the door for the rovers that followed: Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance. A 100-metre drive started a revolution.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Pathfinder landed with airbags and rolled out the tiny Sojourner rover, then explain why the landing style mattered.

name: Spirit and Opportunity
teaser: Spirit and Opportunity were NASA's twin Mars rovers, and their story is one of endurance beyond all expectations. Both landed in January 2004 with a planned mission of 90 days. Spirit roamed Gusev Crater for six years until it became stuck in soft soil and fell silent in 2010. Opportunity exceeded every record, driving more than 45 kilometers across Meridiani Planum for nearly 15 years - a marathon on another world. It found compelling evidence of ancient liquid water: minerals like hematite that form in water, and rocks shaped by it. Opportunity's final message, sent as a planet-wide dust storm killed it in 2018, was a data dump of its last observations. These rovers proved that robots built for months could last for decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the twin rovers searched for Martian water and why Opportunity drove a marathon, then explain their biggest finds.

name: Opportunity's Long Drive
teaser: Opportunity, NASA's Mars rover, was built for 90 days. It survived 15 years. Launched in 2003 and landing in 2004, it kept rolling across the red planet's Meridiani Planum — a record-breaking 45 kilometres in total — while enduring dust storms, winters and crater crossings. It found the first evidence of ancient liquid water on Mars's surface: small spheres of hematite that could only have formed in water. Its last words, sent as a global dust storm choked its solar panels in 2018, were poetic: 'My battery is low and it's getting dark.' It fell silent, a machine that outlived every expectation, a tribute to engineering and stubbornness.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Opportunity survived far beyond its design life and what it found in endurance crater, then explain why it finally stopped.

name: MAVEN
teaser: MAVEN is the Mars orbiter that studies the planet's atmosphere — and its disappearance. The Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution mission, in orbit since 2014, measures how the solar wind strips gas from Mars's atmosphere, ion by ion. Its findings are dramatic: the Sun has been peeling away Mars's air for billions of years, and atmospheric escape explains how a once-warm, wet Mars became the cold desert we see. MAVEN has measured escape rates, watched the atmosphere respond to solar storms, and mapped the loss of hydrogen and oxygen. It's solving the mystery of where Mars's air went — and the answer is blowing in the wind.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how MAVEN studies how solar wind strips Mars's atmosphere, then explain what that means for the planet's wet past.

name: MESSENGER at Mercury
teaser: MESSENGER was the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury — the closest planet to the Sun, where it's brutally hot and the gravity is tricky. It made history in 2011 and spent four years mapping the planet: photographing its craters, measuring its iron core, and discovering water ice in shadowed polar craters and a surprisingly dynamic magnetosphere. Before MESSENGER, Mercury was the least-known planet; it left as the most thoroughly mapped. Running out of fuel in 2015, it ended its mission by crashing into the surface it had studied — a final, deliberate impact on the planet that had become its home.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what MESSENGER found at Mercury including water ice in shadowed craters, then explain how it ended its mission.

name: BepiColombo
teaser: BepiColombo is a joint European-Japanese mission on its way to Mercury, the least-explored rocky planet. Launched in 2018, it carries two orbiters: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Japan's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, which will study the planet's surface, interior, and magnetic field from complementary perspectives. The journey is slow because reaching Mercury's deep gravity well requires multiple flybys - of Earth, Venus, and Mercury itself - to bleed off speed. BepiColombo will arrive in the mid-2020s and begin the most detailed study of Mercury ever attempted, probing its giant iron core, its mysterious magnetic field, and its polar ice. It is named after Giuseppe Colombo, who first explained Mercury's odd 3:2 rotation.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the two-in-one BepiColombo mission and what it aims to reveal about Mercury, then explain why it takes years to arrive.

name: The Galileo Mission
teaser: The Galileo mission was the first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter, and it delivered one of the most dramatic moments in planetary exploration: dropping a probe into the giant planet's atmosphere. In December 1995, the probe plunged into Jupiter's clouds, surviving 150 times Earth's pressure before being crushed, sending back the first direct measurements of the atmosphere - surprising dryness, intense winds, and a turbulent interior. The orbiter then spent eight years studying Jupiter and its moons, discovering that Europa hides a global ocean beneath its ice, that Io's volcanoes are the most active in the solar system, and that Ganymede has its own magnetic field. Galileo's observations rewrote our understanding of the outer solar system.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Galileo orbited Jupiter and dropped a probe into its clouds, then explain what it found about the Galilean moons.

name: Juno's Deep Questions
teaser: Juno is on a mission to understand Jupiter from the inside out — how it formed, what's beneath its clouds, and whether it has a solid core. Since 2016, the solar-powered spacecraft has been diving over Jupiter's poles every 53 days, mapping its gravity and magnetic fields, peering through the clouds with microwave radiometry, and photographing auroras and storms. The results have been stunning: the deep interior shows surprising structure, the magnetic field is lumpier than expected, and the poles are covered in swirling cyclones. Juno is answering the fundamental question of how the solar system's giant planet — and by extension our solar system — came to be.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what Juno measures about Jupiter's interior and origin, then explain how gravity data reveals the deep structure.

name: The Huygens Landing
teaser: Huygens was the probe that landed on Titan — the first and only landing on a moon beyond Mars. Released by the Cassini spacecraft in January 2005, it descended by parachute through Titan's thick orange haze, photographing the surface and sampling the atmosphere for 2.5 hours. It landed on a surprisingly solid surface — a pebbly plain of water ice and hydrocarbon sand — and transmitted data until its batteries died. The descent revealed river channels and a landscape shaped by methane rain. Huygens proved that landing on an alien moon is possible, and its data made Titan one of the most fascinating places in the solar system.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Huygens parachuted through Titan's haze and landed, then explain what its hour of data revealed.

name: Voyager 2 at Neptune
teaser: Voyager 2's Neptune flyby in August 1989 was the final stop of the Grand Tour — and the last time any spacecraft has visited Neptune. The flyby revealed a world of stunning blue beauty: supersonic winds, a Great Dark Spot, and the moon Triton with its nitrogen geysers. Voyager 2 approached within 5,000 km of Neptune's north pole, imaging the planet and its moons in detail before heading out of the solar system. It remains the only spacecraft ever to reach Neptune, more than three decades later. The ice giants — Uranus and Neptune — are the least explored planets, and their secrets wait for a new visitor.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what Voyager 2 found at Neptune including its winds and moons, then explain why it remains the only visit.

name: The DART Impact
teaser: DART was the first planetary defense test — proof that humanity can move an asteroid. In September 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test spacecraft deliberately slammed into the small moon Dimorphos at 22,000 km/h, crashing into it at about 6.6 km/s. The impact shortened Dimorphos's orbit around its parent asteroid by 32 minutes — far more than expected, as the ejected debris added extra thrust. The mission proved that a kinetic impactor can nudge an asteroid off course, the key technique for deflecting a future threat. DART was a kamikaze with a purpose: protecting Earth, tested on a rock that never threatened us.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how DART deliberately hit the moon Dimorphos and changed its orbit, then explain why the test mattered for planetary defense.

name: Lucy: The Trojan Explorer
teaser: Lucy is NASA's mission to Jupiter's Trojan asteroids — the fossils of planet formation. Launched in October 2021, it will visit more asteroids than any mission before it: a main-belt asteroid and seven Trojans, the swarms that share Jupiter's orbit at the L4 and L5 Lagrange points. The Trojans are believed to be leftover building blocks from the solar system's formation, preserved for 4.5 billion years. Lucy will study their geology, composition and origins, named after the fossil hominin that reshaped our understanding of human evolution — fittingly, the mission aims to understand the evolution of the solar system itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Lucy will fly by multiple Trojan asteroids and why they are fossils of the early solar system, then explain its long tour.

name: Psyche: The Metal World
teaser: Psyche is a mission to a metal world — a 226-km-wide asteroid that appears to be mostly iron and nickel, possibly the exposed core of a shattered protoplanet. Launched in October 2023, it will orbit the asteroid Psyche in 2029 and study it with cameras, spectrometers and a magnetometer, testing the theory that it's the core of an early planet whose outer layers were stripped away by collisions. If confirmed, Psyche would give us a direct look at the interior of a planet — the closest thing to a planetary core we could ever visit. It's a journey to the heart of a world.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the metal asteroid Psyche and why its exposure of a core fascinates scientists, then explain what the mission hopes to learn.

name: InSight on Mars
teaser: InSight was the geophysicist on Mars — the mission that listened to the red planet's heartbeat. Landing in 2018, it deployed the first seismometer on another planet and detected over 1,300 marsquakes, revealing Mars's interior for the first time: a thick crust, a molten core and a deep mantle. It also measured heat flow from the planet's interior, though its 'mole' heat probe famously struggled to dig. InSight's data rewrote Mars's internal structure — its core is larger and less dense than expected — and its marsquake catalogue continues to be analyzed. The mission ended in 2022 when dust covered its solar panels, but its legacy is a new science: Martian seismology.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how InSight detected marsquakes and probed Mars's interior, then explain what the seismic data revealed about the core.

name: ExoMars
teaser: ExoMars is Europe's ambitious program to search for life on Mars. The Trace Gas Orbiter has been in orbit since 2016, mapping methane and other trace gases in the atmosphere with exquisite sensitivity. The Rosalind Franklin rover, delayed but scheduled for launch, will drill two metres into the Martian subsurface — deeper than any rover before — to seek organic molecules preserved from a time when Mars was wet. The program aims to answer whether Mars ever hosted life, and whether it might still. The drill's depth is key: radiation at the surface destroys organics, but two metres down, they may survive.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the ExoMars program and its goal to drill beneath the Martian surface, then explain why the subsurface is the best bet.

name: Europa Clipper
teaser: Europa Clipper is NASA's flagship mission to the most promising place for life in the solar system — Jupiter's moon Europa, with its hidden ocean. Launching in 2024, it will make dozens of close flybys of Europa, mapping its ice shell, probing its ocean with radar, and analyzing the plumes of material that may vent from beneath the ice. The spacecraft will fly through Europa's harsh radiation environment with careful shielding, its huge solar arrays extending longer than a basketball court. Clipper will answer whether Europa's ocean has the ingredients for life — and prepare the way for a future lander that could touch the ice.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Europa Clipper will study the icy moon's ocean and ice shell, then explain what signs of habitability it will seek.

name: Dragonfly
teaser: Dragonfly is a mission that sounds like science fiction: a rotorcraft - a flying drone the size of a car - that will explore Saturn's moon Titan, the only moon with a thick atmosphere and rivers and lakes of liquid methane. Launching in the late 2020s, Dragonfly will land in 2034 and hop from site to site, flying tens of kilometers between landings. Titan's dense atmosphere and low gravity make flight easy, and its surface hides organic chemistry that may mirror the prebiotic Earth. Dragonfly will sample the sand dunes and impact craters, searching for the building blocks of life. It is the first rotorcraft ever sent to another world, and it could rewrite our understanding of where life can begin.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Dragonfly will fly between Titan's dunes and explore prebiotic chemistry, then explain why a drone suits Titan.

name: Chandrayaan
teaser: Chandrayaan is India's lunar program, a series of missions that have made the nation a lunar power. Chandrayaan-1, in 2008, discovered water molecules on the Moon — a finding that reshaped lunar science. Chandrayaan-2, in 2019, reached lunar orbit and released a lander that crashed near the pole, but its orbiter continues to map the Moon. Chandrayaan-3, in August 2023, achieved the historic soft landing near the lunar south pole — the first spacecraft ever to land there — and its rover Pragyan explored the region, confirming sulphur and other elements in the soil. India became the fourth nation to land on the Moon, and its program keeps climbing.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how India's Chandrayaan missions explored the Moon including a landing near the south pole, then explain why that region matters.

name: The V-2 Rocket
teaser: The V-2 was the world's first long-range ballistic missile — and the ancestor of every space rocket. Built by Wernher von Braun's team in Nazi Germany and first launched in 1942, it could carry a warhead 300 km, reaching the edge of space. After the war, captured V-2s and their engineers — including von Braun — were taken to the US and USSR, where they formed the foundation of both countries' rocket programs. The V-2 was used as a research rocket, photographing the first images of Earth from space, and its engine designs evolved into the missiles and launchers of the space age. A weapon of war, repurposed as the key to space.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the V-2 became the first rocket to reach space and how its engineers shaped the space age, then explain its dark legacy.

name: The R-7 Rocket
teaser: The R-7 was the rocket that opened the space age. Developed by Sergei Korolev's Soviet team as an intercontinental missile, its first successful flight in 1957 carried Sputnik 1 into orbit — the first artificial satellite. Modified R-7s launched every Soviet first: Laika, Gagarin, Tereshkova, the first spacewalk and the first space station. The R-7 family, called Soyuz, is still flying today — the most-launched rocket family in history, with over 1,900 flights. Its distinctive cluster of four strap-on boosters is one of the most iconic silhouettes in engineering. A missile design from 1957, still lifting humans to space 65 years later.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the R-7 launched Sputnik and remains in service today, then explain why its design proved so durable.

name: The Saturn V
teaser: The Saturn V is still the largest, most powerful rocket ever flown to orbit. Built for the Apollo program under Wernher von Braun, it stood 110 metres tall — taller than a 30-storey building — and produced 34.5 million newtons of thrust, more than all the aircraft in World War II combined. It flew 13 times from 1967 to 1973, and every one succeeded. The Saturn V carried Apollo crews to the Moon, including all six landings, and launched the Skylab space station. Its F-1 engines remain the most powerful liquid-fueled engines ever built. Half a century later, no operational rocket has matched it — a giant that set the bar for everything since.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the Saturn V became the most powerful rocket ever flown, then explain why it has never been matched.

name: Saturn V Stage by Stage
teaser: The Saturn V was built in three stages, each with a job. The S-IC first stage, powered by five F-1 engines, lifted the 3,000-tonne rocket off the pad and burned for 2.5 minutes, consuming fuel at 15 tonnes per second. The S-II second stage, with five J-2 engines, carried it to the edge of space. The S-IVB third stage put the spacecraft into orbit, then fired again for translunar injection — the burn that sent the crew to the Moon. Each stage was discarded when spent, a falling giant. The whole choreography lasted 11 minutes to orbit and worked on every single flight. Staging was the key that made the Moon reachable.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how each Saturn V stage worked from launch to lunar injection, then explain why stage separation is so critical.

name: The Soyuz Rocket
teaser: The Soyuz is the most-flown rocket in history — over 1,900 launches since 1966, with a remarkable safety record. Its design is a direct descendant of the R-7, the first ICBM, with a central core and four strap-on boosters forming the distinctive cluster. Soyuz rockets have launched Sputnik, Gagarin and every Soviet and Russian crewed mission, and they remain the workhorse for the International Space Station, flying astronauts from dozens of nations. The Soyuz spacecraft — the capsule it launches — is equally legendary: the longest-serving crewed spacecraft in history, upgraded continuously but recognizably the same design for six decades. In spaceflight, some classics never retire.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the Soyuz rocket has flown for decades carrying crews, then explain why its simple design endures.

name: Falcon 9
teaser: The Falcon 9 is the rocket that made landing routine — the first orbital-class booster to fly repeatedly. SpaceX's workhorse has launched over 400 times since 2010, carrying satellites, cargo and crew, and its first stage now lands itself on drone ships or pads with remarkable regularity — some boosters have flown 20 times or more. Falcon 9's reusability cut launch costs dramatically, transforming the economics of space, and its Dragon capsule ferries astronauts to the ISS. The rocket's landing legs and grid fins are now icons. What was science fiction in 2010 — a rocket that comes home — is now a Tuesday occurrence.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Falcon 9 changed the economics of launch with reusable boosters, then explain what a booster landing involves.

name: The Ariane Rockets
teaser: Ariane is Europe's family of launch vehicles, flying since 1979 and launching over 250 missions. Ariane 4 was the commercial workhorse of the 1990s, launching most of the world's big satellites; Ariane 5 flew for 27 years, sending everything from Galileo navigation satellites to the James Webb Space Telescope into space. The new Ariane 6 flew its first launch in 2024. Ariane rockets launch from the European spaceport at Kourou, French Guiana, near the equator — the perfect spot for reaching geostationary orbit. For 45 years, Ariane has been Europe's reliable ticket to space, and it keeps flying.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the Ariane family and Europe's role in launching satellites, then explain why Ariane 5 was so reliable.

name: Rocket Lab's Electron
teaser: Electron is the small rocket that democratized space — Rocket Lab's 18-metre rocket that launches shoebox-sized satellites for a fraction of the cost of its big siblings. Since 2017, it has launched over 50 missions from New Zealand, delivering CubeSats and small payloads to precise orbits, with a unique twist: its first stage falls back to Earth under parachute and is caught mid-air by a helicopter. Electron has even sent a small probe, CAPSTONE, to lunar orbit, and Rocket Lab plans a bigger rocket, Neutron, for medium payloads. Small rockets are opening space to small teams — and Electron is leading the charge.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Electron serves small satellites with frequent launches, then explain why its engine is printed.

name: World Launch Sites
teaser: Rockets leave Earth from a handful of carefully chosen places. The ideal launch site sits near the equator, where Earth's spin gives rockets a free speed boost — that's why Kourou in French Guiana and the Kennedy Space Center in Florida are so valuable. Sites need safety zones downrange, good weather and political stability. The major players: Cape Canaveral in the US, Baikonur in Kazakhstan, Kourou in Europe's French Guiana, Vandenberg for polar orbits, and new Chinese, Indian and commercial pads. Every launch site is a compromise between geography, physics and politics — and each one is the gateway to space for its nation.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the world's major launch sites and why location matters, then explain the advantage of launching near the equator.

name: Cape Canaveral
teaser: Cape Canaveral is the historic heart of American spaceflight — the launch site for every Apollo mission, every Space Shuttle flight, and today, the private rockets of SpaceX and its rivals. The Cape was chosen in the 1940s for its remote location and its position: launches head east over the Atlantic, using Earth's rotation for speed. It's witnessed every American milestone — Alan Shepard's first flight, John Glenn's orbit, the Moon landings, the shuttle era — and it's now the busiest launch site on Earth, with launches happening weekly. The skyline of launch pads along the Atlantic coast is the monument of the space age.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Cape Canaveral became the heart of American spaceflight, then explain why it was chosen.

name: Baikonur Cosmodrome
teaser: Baikonur is the world's first and busiest spaceport — a vast complex in the steppes of Kazakhstan from which the space age was launched. Sputnik flew from here in 1957, Gagarin in 1961, and it remains the launch site for every Russian crewed mission and the Soyuz rocket that has carried astronauts for six decades. It's where the first human orbits, the first spacewalks and the first space stations began. Baikonur is leased by Russia from Kazakhstan, a unique Cold War arrangement that survives to this day, and its launch pads — including Gagarin's Start — are monuments of history. The desert around it is littered with fallen rocket stages, a landscape of discarded boosters.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Baikonur's role from Sputnik to the ISS, then explain why its location was kept secret for years.

name: Kourou and the Equator
teaser: Kourou, in French Guiana on the north coast of South America, is Europe's spaceport — and one of the best launch sites on Earth. At just 5 degrees north of the equator, it maximizes the free speed from Earth's rotation, giving rockets a boost they can't get from higher-latitude sites. The European Space Agency has launched its Ariane rockets from Kourou since 1979, joined by Vega and the Russian Soyuz, and the site hosted the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope in 2021. The jungle setting, with launch pads rising from the rainforest, is one of the most striking industrial landscapes in the world. Geography made Kourou the perfect front door to space.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why the French Guiana spaceport sits near the equator and what that gives launches, then explain the spin boost.

name: Rocket Engine Cycles
teaser: Inside every rocket engine is a plumbing miracle. The fuel and oxidizer must be pumped into the combustion chamber at enormous rates and pressures — the F-1 engine pumped 15 tonnes per second — and the pumps themselves must be driven. Open-cycle engines divert some exhaust to spin the pumps; closed-cycle, or staged-combustion, engines feed all the exhaust through, gaining efficiency at the cost of complexity. The engines of the Raptor, Merlin and RS-25 each use different cycles, and the choice trades power, efficiency and reliability. A rocket engine is basically a controlled bomb, and its plumbing is the engineering that keeps the explosion pointed the right way.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rocket engines feed fuel and oxidizer and why some use staged combustion, then explain the trade-offs.

name: Thrust and Weight
teaser: A rocket can only lift off if its thrust is greater than its weight — the thrust-to-weight ratio must exceed one. At liftoff, the Saturn V's ratio was about 1.2: the engines pushed 20 percent harder than the rocket's weight, so it climbed slowly at first, then accelerated as fuel burned off. Modern rockets like the Falcon 9 and Starship have higher ratios, lifting off faster. The ratio changes constantly during flight as propellant is consumed — a rocket's acceleration grows as it lightens. The physics is unforgiving: thrust less than weight, and the rocket just sits there, shaking and burning fuel. Every launch is a battle against your own weight.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what thrust-to-weight ratio means and why rockets are mostly fuel, then explain how TWR changes during flight.

name: Max Q
teaser: Max Q — maximum dynamic pressure — is the most stressful moment of a launch. As a rocket accelerates through the lower atmosphere, the air pushes against it with growing force, peaking at about 10 to 14 km altitude, then falling as the air thins. The combination of high speed and thick air strains the vehicle's structure to its limit, so engineers throttle the engines down as they approach Max Q to reduce stress. It's the moment when the whole rocket groans under the load — visible in the shaking of launch videos. Get past Max Q, and the atmosphere's grip loosens; the rocket's climb gets easier. Every rocket passes through the wall.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what Max Q is and why rockets throttle through it, then explain what happens to the structure at peak pressure.

name: Breaking the Sound Barrier
teaser: The sound barrier is not a barrier at all — it's simply the point where an object reaches the speed of sound, about 1,235 km/h at sea level. When a rocket or aircraft passes through, it compresses air into a shockwave that we hear as a sonic boom. Early pilots thought the 'barrier' was a wall that would destroy any aircraft, and several died trying to cross it — until Chuck Yeager broke it in 1947. Rockets break the sound barrier seconds after liftoff, and the boom thunders across the launch site. Supersonic flight is now routine: the boom is just the sound of the air being parted at the speed of sound.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what the sound barrier is and why breaking it creates a boom, then explain how it relates to rocket launch.

name: Rocket Sled Tests
teaser: Before a rocket carries humans, its escape system must be tested — and one of the most dramatic test methods is the rocket sled. Sleds accelerate a full-size crew capsule down a track at hundreds of kilometres per hour, then fire the escape tower, yanking the capsule to safety mid-ride. The tests simulate the worst case: a rocket failing on the pad or early in ascent, with the crew needing to be pulled away in seconds. SpaceX and NASA ran sled tests before the Crew Dragon's first crewed flight, filming the escape tower firing at the exact moment of crisis. The sled is a crash-test dummy's ride to space — proof that when the worst happens, the crew can get out.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rocket sleds test ejection and escape systems, then explain why such violent tests are worth it.

name: Blue Origin
teaser: Blue Origin, founded by Jeff Bezos in 2000, is the quiet giant of American spaceflight. Its New Shepard rocket flies suborbital tourism flights to the edge of space, carrying passengers including Bezos himself and Star Trek's William Shatner, who at 90 became the oldest person in space. Its New Glenn rocket, first launched in 2025, is a heavy-lift vehicle for orbital missions, and its BE-4 engines power United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket. Blue Origin's motto — 'Gradatim Ferociter', 'Step by step, ferociously' — reflects its patient approach. The company's long-term vision is millions of people living and working in space, starting with orbital habitats.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Blue Origin's suborbital tourism and heavy rocket plans, then explain how it competes in the private space race.

name: Neutron: The Medium Lifter
teaser: Neutron is Rocket Lab's next-generation rocket — a medium-lift vehicle designed to deliver the 'megaconstellations' of small satellites that are reshaping space. First planned for launch in 2025, it stands 43 metres tall, uses a reusable first stage that returns to a landing barge, and features an unusual carbon-composite body. Its Archimedes engines are designed for rapid reuse, and it's aimed at the market between small rockets like Electron and heavy lifters like Falcon 9. Rocket Lab is betting that the satellite revolution needs a middle-weight workhorse — and Neutron is its answer. The space industry is building a ladder of rockets for every job.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Rocket Lab's Neutron rocket and its reusable design, then explain what role it aims to play.

name: Vulcan Centaur
teaser: Vulcan is United Launch Alliance's next-generation rocket — the successor to the legendary Atlas and Delta families. It flew its first mission in January 2024, carrying Astrobotic's Peregrine lunar lander, and it's designed to launch the most demanding missions: national security payloads, crewed spacecraft and interplanetary probes. Vulcan's first stage is powered by Blue Origin's BE-4 methane engines, and its second stage can be upgraded with extra thrust. It's also notable for its SMART reuse plan, which recovers the engines after flight. Vulcan marks the transition of one of America's oldest launch companies into the reusable era — a classic rocket for a new space age.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Vulcan Centaur rocket and what it replaces, then explain why methane fuel is part of its design.

name: Transits of Venus
teaser: A transit of Venus happens when Venus passes directly between Earth and the Sun, appearing as a small black dot crossing the Sun's face. It's one of the rarest predictable celestial events — transits come in pairs eight years apart, separated by more than a century. The 1761 and 1769 transits were used to measure the distance from Earth to the Sun, with expeditions sent around the world, including James Cook's voyage to Tahiti. The 1882 transit produced the first photographs; the last one, in 2012, was watched by millions online. The next won't occur until 2117. A tiny dot of shadow, a century of waiting.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how transits of Venus let astronomers measure the solar system, then explain why they come in pairs eight years apart.

name: Transits of Mercury
teaser: Mercury transits are the quiet siblings of Venus transits — Mercury, the solar system's smallest planet, passes in front of the Sun as a tiny black dot. They happen about 13 times a century, when Mercury crosses between Earth and the Sun. Transits last several hours, and observing them requires proper solar filters — never look at the Sun directly. The 1631 transit, predicted by Kepler, confirmed planetary theory; the 2006 and 2016 transits were streamed online and photographed by satellites. Mercury's transit is a reminder of the solar system's clockwork: a planet the size of a dot, crossing a star, right on schedule, as it has for billions of years.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how often Mercury crosses the Sun and how to watch safely, then explain why it taught astronomers about orbits.

name: Occultations
teaser: An occultation happens when one celestial object passes in front of another, hiding it. The Moon occults stars constantly as it moves across the sky; planets occult stars and other planets; and asteroids occult stars in brief blinks visible only from narrow paths on Earth. Occultations are more than beautiful — they're scientific tools. Lunar occultations helped map the Moon's limb; asteroid occultations let astronomers measure the shapes of distant rocks; and the 1977 occultation of a star by Uranus led to the discovery of its rings. Timing a star's blink from different locations can even reveal the size and shape of a distant world. When the sky hides something, astronomy pays attention.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what an occultation is and why astronomers time them precisely, then explain how they measure asteroids and moons.

name: Conjunctions
teaser: A conjunction is when two celestial objects appear close together in the sky — the planets' version of a meeting. Venus and Jupiter conjunctions are the showstoppers, the two brightest planets shining together so close they almost touch, and the Great Conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn, which happens every 20 years, is a sky event people travel for. The 2020 Great Conjunction brought the two giants within a tenth of a degree. Conjunctions are purely a matter of perspective — the objects are millions of kilometres apart — but they're among the most beautiful sights in the sky, and they remind us that the solar system dances to a shared rhythm.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover what a planetary conjunction is and how to predict one, then explain why the planets only appear close.

name: Sun Dogs and Halos
teaser: Sun dogs, or parhelia, are bright spots that appear beside the Sun — two glowing patches flanking it, sometimes with halos and arcs. They're caused by ice crystals high in the atmosphere refracting sunlight: hexagonal plates drift down, bending light at 22 degrees, creating the spots at that angle on either side of the Sun. Sun dogs often appear in cold, clear weather and can be brilliantly colourful — red on the inside, blue on the outside. They're seen by anyone who looks up on a frosty day, and they're one of the most common sky illusions, more striking than the halo itself. The sky is full of ice-crystal mirrors.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how ice crystals create sundogs and halos, then explain why they often appear in cold weather.

name: Rainbows
teaser: Rainbows are the physics of light and water — and their science is glorious. Sunlight entering a raindrop refracts, reflects off the back, and refracts again, splitting into colours and bending back toward you at about 42 degrees. That's why you never see a rainbow from an airplane the same way, and why each observer sees their own bow — the rainbow moves with you. Double rainbows have the colours reversed; supernumerary bows, faint and pastel, come from light waves interfering. Rainbows are a circle when seen from above — and their physics is the same physics that splits starlight in telescopes. The arc in the sky is a full circle of light, cut off by the ground.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how rainbows form and why each person sees their own, then explain why the order of colors never changes.

name: Moonbows
teaser: A moonbow is a rainbow made by moonlight — a rare, ghostly arc that appears on nights of a bright full Moon, usually near waterfalls or sea spray where fine mist hangs in the air. The physics is identical to a sunlit rainbow, but the light is a million times fainter, so moonbows appear pale and colourless to the eye — long-exposure photographs reveal their colours. The most famous moonbow viewing spots are Yosemite Falls in California, Victoria Falls, and Cumberland Falls in Kentucky. They need a bright Moon low behind you and mist ahead, and the conditions align only a few nights a year. A rainbow of moonlight is one of the sky's quietest, most magical gifts.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what a moonbow is and why it is rare and faint, then explain where the best ones appear.

name: The Green Flash
teaser: The green flash is a rare, brief burst of green light at the exact moment the Sun sets — or rises — over a clear horizon. It happens because the atmosphere bends light like a prism, separating colours: as the Sun's disc slips below the horizon, the last sliver is green, and under perfect conditions, with clean air and a flat horizon, the green flash appears for a second or two. Some observers report it lasting longer or splitting into a green ray. It's not a myth — it's the atmosphere's refraction at work, and the Sun is actually green for a moment every clear sunset. You just have to look at exactly the right second.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the green flash at sunset and why the atmosphere makes it, then explain why it lasts only a second.

name: Crepuscular Rays
teaser: Crepuscular rays are the dramatic 'god rays' that fan out from behind clouds when the Sun is low — shafts of sunlight streaming through gaps in the cloud cover. They're beams of sunlight through holes in the clouds, and they appear to converge toward the Sun because of perspective, like parallel train tracks meeting at the horizon. The shadows between them are cast by the clouds themselves. When the Sun is behind you, the same rays can appear to converge at the anti-solar point — 'anti-crepuscular rays'. They're most common at sunrise and sunset, when the low Sun's light passes through the longest, dustiest path of atmosphere. The sky becomes a cathedral of light.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how crepuscular rays form and why they seem to converge, then explain the perspective trick behind them.

name: Why the Sky Is Blue
teaser: The sky is blue because of scattering — tiny air molecules scatter sunlight in all directions, and they scatter blue light far more than red, because blue has a shorter wavelength. This is Rayleigh scattering, named for Lord Rayleigh, who explained it in 1871. The same physics explains sunsets: at sunset, sunlight passes through more atmosphere, scattering away the blue, leaving the reds and oranges that paint the evening sky. On Mars, the sky is pink because its dust scatters light differently. The colour of a planet's sky is a message about its atmosphere — and ours is blue because the air is made of molecules that love to scatter blue.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why molecules scatter blue light more than red, then explain why sunsets turn orange and red.

name: Twilight Zones
teaser: Twilight is the glow that lingers after sunset and precedes sunrise — the sunlight still illuminating the upper atmosphere while the Sun is below the horizon. Astronomers divide it into three stages. Civil twilight, when the Sun is up to 6 degrees below the horizon, is bright enough for most activities. Nautical twilight, to 12 degrees, is when the horizon is still visible for navigation. Astronomical twilight, to 18 degrees, is when the sky is truly dark — after that, 'night' begins, and the faintest objects become visible. The three twilights matter to photographers, sailors and astronomers alike. The day doesn't end at sunset; it fades in stages.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the three kinds of twilight and when each begins and ends, then explain why astronomers wait for the dark.

name: The Glory
teaser: A glory is a rainbow-like ring of light that appears around your own shadow — most often seen from airplanes, when the plane's shadow falls on a cloud below and is encircled by concentric coloured rings. It's caused by light being backscattered and diffracted by tiny water droplets, a quantum effect that even had physicists puzzling. Glories are the 'Brocken spectre' of mountain lore, where a climber's shadow on the mist is ringed with colour — and the glowing ring around a plane's shadow is the same phenomenon. The most dramatic glories appear on foggy summits and cloud tops. The sky wearing a halo around your shadow is one of the strangest optical gifts in nature.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the colorful glory effect seen from planes and mountains, then explain how cloud droplets make it.

name: Iridescent Clouds
teaser: Iridescent clouds — sometimes called 'cloud rainbows' — are thin clouds showing patches of pastel colour, like oil on water. They form when sunlight is diffracted by tiny, uniformly sized water droplets or ice crystals near the cloud edges. The colours are most vivid in thin, freshly formed clouds — altocumulus, cirrocumulus and lenticular clouds — within a few degrees of the Sun. Iridescence is the sibling of coronas (coloured rings around the Sun or Moon) and appears when the droplets are nearly identical in size, bending light into colours. Look near the Sun's edge through sunglasses and you might catch a cloud glowing pink, green and blue.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why some clouds show pastel colors and where to look for them, then explain the diffraction behind the shimmer.

name: Noctilucent Clouds
teaser: Noctilucent clouds are the highest clouds in Earth's atmosphere — glowing, electric-blue wisps that form about 80 km up, at the edge of space, where other clouds can't exist. They're made of ice crystals coating meteor dust, and they're visible only in deep twilight, when the Sun is below the horizon but still lighting these lofty layers. They're a modern phenomenon: first reported in 1885 after the Krakatoa eruption, they've become more frequent and widespread since, possibly a sign of climate change. They appear in summer at high latitudes, drifting in from the polar regions. Silver-blue clouds at the edge of space — the sky's rarest light show.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the highest clouds on Earth and why they glow after sunset, then explain what links them to space dust.

name: The Northern Lights
teaser: The aurora borealis — the northern lights — is the sky's greatest light show: curtains, arcs and rays of green, red and purple dancing across the polar night. It begins at the Sun, which flings charged particles in the solar wind. When they reach Earth, the magnetic field channels them toward the poles, where they crash into oxygen and nitrogen atoms in the upper atmosphere, making them glow like a neon sign — green and red from oxygen, blue and purple from nitrogen. Auroras appear most often in an oval around the magnetic poles, and during strong solar storms they can be seen far from the Arctic. The lights of the polar sky have awed humans for millennia — and science finally explains the magic.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how solar particles make auroras and why they appear near the poles, then explain the green and red colors.

name: The Southern Lights
teaser: The aurora australis is the southern twin of the northern lights — the same solar particles, the same glowing curtains, but painted over Antarctica and the southern ocean. It's seen from Tasmania, New Zealand's South Island, southern Australia and Antarctica, and its colours and shapes match its northern sibling: greens and reds from oxygen, blues from nitrogen. Because the southern hemisphere has fewer landmasses near the auroral oval, the southern lights are photographed less often — but from the ice of Antarctica, they're a spectacle of uninhabited majesty. During strong solar storms, both auroras blaze at once, and satellites can photograph the two polar crowns of light simultaneously.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the southern aurora and where it is best seen, then explain how it mirrors the northern lights.

name: Auroras on Other Planets
teaser: Earth isn't the only planet with auroras — Jupiter and Saturn put on far more powerful shows. Jupiter's auroras are the strongest in the solar system, driven by its giant magnetic field and the volcanic moon Io, which injects charged particles into the Jovian magnetosphere. They glow in ultraviolet, X-ray and radio, constantly, hundreds of times more energetic than Earth's. Saturn's auroras are calmer, shaped by its rings. Even Uranus and Neptune show auroral glows, and auroras have been detected on Mars. Every magnetized planet dances with the solar wind in its own way. The northern lights are a local version of a universal phenomenon.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Jupiter and Saturn produce their own auroras, then explain what Hubble's images of them revealed.

name: Solar Storms and the Aurora
teaser: Auroras flare when the Sun storms. When the Sun hurls a coronal mass ejection — a billion-tonne cloud of magnetized plasma — toward Earth, it slams into our magnetic field, compressing it and pouring particles into the polar zones. The result is auroras that swell, brighten and race toward the equator. During the great geomagnetic storm of May 2024, the strongest in two decades, auroras were photographed from Florida, Mexico, India and southern Europe — places that never see them. The storms that drive auroras can also disrupt satellites, power grids and radio. The beautiful lights are the visible face of a magnetic storm — the sky's glow is the danger warning.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how coronal mass ejections supercharge auroras, then explain why strong storms push the lights toward the equator.

name: Airglow
teaser: Airglow is the sky's faint self-light — a permanent, dim glow of the atmosphere itself, glowing even on the darkest, moonless nights. It's produced by chemical reactions in the upper atmosphere: oxygen atoms recombine and emit green and red light, sodium from meteor dust glows yellow, and hydroxyl molecules radiate in infrared. Airglow is why a truly black night sky still isn't perfectly black — and it's the noise floor that faint-object astronomers must fight. It's strongest about 90 to 100 km up, and long-exposure photographs from dark sites often show it as a faint green band across the horizon. The sky isn't just lit from above — it glows from within.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what airglow is and why the atmosphere glows even at night, then explain how it confuses and aids astronomers.

name: The Zodiac Band
teaser: The zodiac is the band of sky through which the Sun, Moon and planets all travel — a belt about 8 degrees wide, centered on the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path. It exists because the planets orbit the Sun in roughly the same flat plane, which we see edge-on. The band is divided into the twelve zodiac constellations — Aries through Pisces — and has been central to astronomy and astrology for thousands of years. The Moon and planets never stray far from the zodiac, which is why they're always found in the same strip of sky. Ancient sky-watchers noticed this band and built calendars, myths and religions around it. The zodiac is the stage where the solar system's actors perform.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why the Moon and planets all travel near the zodiac band, then explain the role of the solar system's flat disk.

name: Arcturus
teaser: Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere and the fourth-brightest in the entire night sky — an orange giant about 37 light-years away. It's most visible in spring, riding high in the evening sky, and you can find it by following the arc of the Big Dipper's handle: 'arc to Arcturus.' It's older and larger than the Sun, a red giant in the making, and it moves through space fast, with its own cluster of stars streaming along with it. Arcturus has a famous story: its light, focused at the 1933 Chicago World's Fair, was used to open the fair by switching on its floodlights. A star that turned on the lights.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how to find Arcturus and why it is moving fast through the galaxy, then explain what its orange color reveals.

name: Aldebaran
teaser: Aldebaran is the fiery orange eye of Taurus the Bull — the brightest star in the constellation and one of the easiest red giants to spot. About 65 light-years away, it's a K-type giant, cooler and redder than the Sun but far larger and brighter. It sits right in the V-shaped Hyades star cluster, though it's actually not a member — it's a foreground star that happens to lie in the same line of sight. Its name comes from the Arabic for 'the follower', because it follows the Pleiades across the sky. In winter skies, the bull's orange eye glows unmistakably between Orion and the Pleiades.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Aldebaran and how to find it near the Pleiades, then explain why it is a red giant compared with the Sun.

name: Antares
teaser: Antares is the red heart of Scorpius — a huge red supergiant about 550 light-years away, so large that if it replaced the Sun, it would swallow the orbit of Mars. Its name means 'rival of Mars' (anti-Ares), because its orange-red colour and brightness make it a Martian lookalike in the summer sky. Antares is near the end of its life and will eventually explode as a supernova, shining brighter than the Moon for a time. It has a small, greenish companion star that's a beautiful sight in telescopes. The heart of the scorpion is one of the sky's most dramatic stars — a dying giant visible to the naked eye.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Antares got its name from rivaling Mars in color, then explain why it will end in a supernova.

name: Deneb
teaser: Deneb is the brilliant tail star of Cygnus the Swan — one of the most luminous stars in the galaxy, shining with the light of about 200,000 Suns. It's part of the Summer Triangle, along with Vega and Altair, and it anchors the Northern Cross of Cygnus. Deneb is a white supergiant about 2,600 light-years away — so far that its true brilliance is staggering: if it were as close as Vega, it would shine as bright as the full Moon. Its name comes from the Arabic for 'tail', and the Milky Way runs right through Cygnus, making the region around Deneb a rich field for binoculars. The swan's tail is a cosmic searchlight.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Deneb and why it is one of the most luminous stars we see, then explain how distance makes its brightness deceptive.

name: Altair
teaser: Altair is one of the brightest stars in the summer sky and one of the closest to Earth at just 17 light-years — the nearest of the Summer Triangle stars. It's a fast spinner, rotating once every 9 hours, so fast that it's visibly flattened at the poles, like a spinning ball of taffy. Altair is the head of the constellation Aquila the Eagle, and its name comes from the Arabic for 'flying eagle'. It's part of the Summer Triangle, the easiest landmark of the northern summer sky, along with Vega and Deneb. Its proximity makes it a prime target for studying stellar structure — a nearby star with secrets to tell.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Altair and its rapid spin, then explain how rotation flattens the star.

name: Castor and Pollux
teaser: Castor and Pollux are the twin stars of Gemini — though they're not actually twins at all. Pollux is an orange giant about 34 light-years away, the 17th-brightest star in the sky; Castor, slightly fainter, is a spectacular multiple star system of six stars orbiting in pairs, about 52 light-years away. In Greek myth, they were the twins Castor and Pollux, one mortal and one immortal, placed together in the sky. Pollux made news in 2006 with the discovery of a planet orbiting it. The two 'twins' look similar to the eye but are physically very different — a celestial joke about identity.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Castor is a complex multiple system while Pollux is a single giant, then explain how the pair got their twin story.

name: Fomalhaut
teaser: Fomalhaut is the loneliest bright star in the sky — a brilliant white star in the southern constellation Piscis Austrinus, visible from northern latitudes only in autumn, surrounded by emptiness. It's about 25 light-years away and hosts a spectacular debris disk — a ring of dust and comets, the first extrasolar disk photographed in visible light. The star's nickname, the 'Autumn Star', marks the season; and it was one of the four 'royal stars' of ancient Persian astronomy. In 2008, astronomers announced a planet orbiting Fomalhaut, Fomalhaut b — later revealed to be a cloud of debris, not a planet. The lone star keeps its secrets.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Fomalhaut and its planet-forming debris disk, then explain why its planets are hard to confirm.

name: Epsilon Eridani
teaser: Epsilon Eridani is a star system 10.5 light-years away that reads like a blueprint of our own solar system: a Sun-like star (though younger and dimmer), a disk of debris, two asteroid-belt-like rings, and a planet — Epsilon Eridani b, a giant about the mass of Jupiter. It's been a fixture of science fiction — it's a major setting in the Star Trek universe, home of the Vulcans in the expanded canon — but its real appeal is scientific: it's the closest system with a structure that resembles ours, young enough to catch planetary formation in the act. The nearest planetary system to our own is a mirror of our past.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Epsilon Eridani and the worlds and belts around it, then explain why it is a target for planet hunting.

name: Tau Ceti
teaser: Tau Ceti is one of the closest Sun-like stars to Earth, just 11.9 light-years away, and it's been a favourite in science fiction as a destination for interstellar missions. It's older than the Sun, stable and metal-rich, making it a promising target in the search for habitable planets. Astronomers have detected at least four planets around it, including candidates in or near the habitable zone — though some may be too massive or too eccentric to be comfortably habitable. Tau Ceti appears in classic novels, TV shows and games as humanity's first interstellar colony. The real star is waiting for a closer look.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Tau Ceti and why it matters for the search for life, then explain what makes it similar to the Sun.

name: Barnard's Star
teaser: Barnard's Star is a red dwarf just 6 light-years away, and it has the fastest apparent motion of any star in the sky — it moves across the sky by almost 10 arcseconds a year, the width of the full Moon in 180 years. It was discovered in 1916 by E. E. Barnard, who realized it was flying through the galaxy's neighbourhood. In 2018, astronomers announced a super-Earth planet around it, Barnard's Star b, later refined and possibly joined by others. It's the closest single star system to the Sun, and it's a prime target for future interstellar probes. A swift little star with a big future.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover why Barnard's Star moves faster across our sky than any other and what orbits it, then explain its long history of false planet claims.

name: Wolf 359
teaser: Wolf 359 is a tiny red dwarf just 7.9 light-years away — one of the dimmest and smallest stars known, shining with only 0.1 percent of the Sun's light. It was discovered photographically in 1919, when its rapid motion revealed its proximity. Despite its faintness, it's a classic science-fiction battleground — in Star Trek, the Battle of Wolf 359 was one of the franchise's defining disasters. In reality, Wolf 359 is a flare star that occasionally brightens dramatically, and it may host planets, hinted at by its wobble. The star next door is a whisper of a sun — but it's one of our closest neighbours.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Wolf 359 and why it is among the closest stars despite its dimness, then explain why red dwarfs dominate nearby space.

name: Sirius B
teaser: Sirius B is the white dwarf companion of Sirius, the brightest star in our night sky — a dense ember the size of Earth holding about the mass of the Sun. It orbits Sirius every 50 years, and in 1915 astronomers realized this faint companion was a new kind of star: matter so compressed that a teaspoon weighs tonnes. That discovery launched the study of white dwarfs and quantum physics. Sirius B is about 10,000 times fainter than its brilliant companion, and seeing it through a telescope is a rite of passage — it takes excellent seeing and patience, since it hides in Sirius's glare. The brightest star in the sky has a ghost at its side.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the tiny white dwarf Sirius B was first seen and why it proved stellar density, then explain how it was found.

name: Procyon
teaser: Procyon is the Little Dog Star — the bright eye of Canis Minor, part of the Winter Triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse. About 11.5 light-years away, it's one of the nearest bright stars, and like Sirius, it has a white dwarf companion, Procyon B, discovered in 1896. Its name comes from the Greek for 'before the dog', because it rises just before Sirius, the Dog Star. In winter evenings, Procyon shines steadily in the south-southeast, marking the little dog that follows the great hunter Orion. It's a quiet, reliable star — but its faint white dwarf companion holds a lesson about stellar evolution.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how to find Procyon and why it also has a white dwarf companion, then explain the star's size and age.

name: Capella
teaser: Capella is the golden star of the winter sky — the sixth-brightest star, and the brightest in the northern constellation Auriga the Charioteer. About 43 light-years away, it's a surprise: what looks like one star is actually a system of four, with two giant yellow stars orbiting each other every 104 days, plus a pair of red dwarfs. The two giants are similar in size and brightness, an unusual 'twin' pair. Capella's name means 'little goat', from the goat that the charioteer carries on his shoulder in Greek myth. In winter, it shines high overhead, one of the most beautiful golden stars in the sky.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover Capella and why it is actually a system of four stars, then explain how spectroscopes revealed the pair.

name: Canopus
teaser: Canopus is the second-brightest star in the entire night sky, after Sirius — a brilliant white supergiant about 310 light-years away, so luminous that it outshines everything else in the southern sky. It's not visible from most of the northern hemisphere, which is why it's less famous than Sirius. Ancient navigators prized it: it was the key star for Polynesian voyagers crossing the Pacific, and its name may come from the Egyptian god of navigation. For the ancient Egyptians, Canopus rose near the Nile's flood season. In the southern sky, the great white star is a landmark that guided sailors across half the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Canopus and why it guided sailors in the southern hemisphere, then explain its enormous luminosity.

name: Mira: The Wonderful Star
teaser: Mira, the 'Wonderful Star', is a pulsating red giant in Cetus the Whale that changes brightness dramatically — over about 332 days it fades from visible to the naked eye down to 10th magnitude, then brightens again, a change of up to 1,500 times. It was the first variable star discovered, in 1596 by David Fabricius, who thought the 'new star' was a nova — until it came back. Mira is also plowing through space at high speed, leaving a 13-light-year-long tail of gas and dust, discovered by the GALEX satellite in 2007. It's the prototype of all Mira-type variables — stars that swell, fade and swell again for eternity.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how Mira's brightness changes over months and why it is the prototype of a class of variables, then explain its trailing tail.

name: The Named Southern Stars
teaser: Achernar, Canopus and their neighbours are the great stars of the far southern sky — a region northern astronomers rarely see. Achernar, the brightest star in Eridanus, is the flattest star known: it spins so fast that its equator bulges out, making it look squashed. Canopus is the sky's second-brightest star. Together with the Southern Cross and the Pointers, they're the landmarks of the southern hemisphere's night, used by sailors and skywatchers for centuries. The southern sky has its own great constellations — Carina, Centaurus, Crux — and its own brilliant stars, a whole hemisphere of wonders that northerners only dream of.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover bright southern stars like Achernar and how they compare with northern ones, then explain why they are invisible to many.

name: The Summer Triangle
teaser: The Summer Triangle is the great landmark of northern summer skies — three brilliant stars, Vega, Deneb and Altair, forming a vast triangle that's visible from city and countryside alike. It's not a constellation but an asterism, spanning three constellations: Lyra, Cygnus and Aquila. In July and August evenings, it stands high overhead, the easiest shape to find in the whole sky. Between its stars runs the Milky Way, and within its borders lie dozens of deep-sky treasures for binoculars — the Ring Nebula, the Dumbbell, the Coathanger. When you find the Summer Triangle, you've found the sky's summer map.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how to spot the Summer Triangle of Vega, Deneb and Altair, then explain why it is a perfect starting point.

name: The Winter Hexagon
teaser: The Winter Hexagon is a giant ring of six of the brightest stars in the sky — Sirius, Procyon, Pollux, Capella, Aldebaran and Rigel — forming a huge circle that dominates winter evenings. Some versions swap in Betelgeuse for Rigel. It's the winter counterpart of the Summer Triangle, and its stars span six constellations. At its centre lies Betelgeuse, the shoulder of Orion, and the constellation of the hunter himself sits inside the hexagon. In January and February, the hexagon is the sky's most magnificent structure — six of the brightest stars in the heavens arranged in a perfect cosmic ring.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how six brilliant stars form the Winter Hexagon, then explain how to hop between them.

name: The Brightest Stars
teaser: The first-magnitude stars are the sky's bright club — the 21 or so stars brighter than magnitude 1.5, visible from anywhere with even a little darkness. They include Sirius, Canopus, Alpha Centauri, Arcturus, Vega, Capella, Rigel, Procyon, Betelgeuse, Aldebaran, Antares, Spica, Pollux, Fomalhaut, Deneb and Regulus, plus a few in the far south. Every one is a giant or near neighbour, and together they trace the sky's brightest patterns. Most cultures built their sky stories around them, and sailors navigated by them. Learn the first-magnitude stars, and you know the sky's backbone forever.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how many stars are first magnitude and what ties them together, then explain why their distances vary wildly.

name: Solar vs Sidereal Day
teaser: A solar day — the 24 hours we live by — is how long it takes the Sun to return to the same spot in the sky. But the stars return a little sooner: the sidereal day, measured against the stars, is 23 hours 56 minutes and 4 seconds. The four-minute difference comes from Earth's orbit: as Earth spins, it also moves along its orbit, so it must turn a little further each day to face the Sun again. That's why the stars rise about 4 minutes earlier each night — and why a given star is visible at different times through the year. Our clocks run on the Sun; astronomers run on the stars.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover the difference between a solar day and a sidereal day, then explain why the stars rise four minutes earlier each night.

name: The Sidereal Year
teaser: The sidereal year is the time it takes Earth to complete one full orbit relative to the stars — 365.256 days. It differs from the tropical year (365.242 days), which is measured against the Sun and drives our calendar, because of precession: Earth's axis slowly wobbles, shifting the equinoxes backward. The difference is only about 20 minutes, but over centuries it accumulates. Astronomers use the sidereal year when tracking stars against the background of the universe; our calendar uses the tropical year to keep seasons aligned. Two ways of measuring the same orbit, each useful in its own way.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how a sidereal year differs from a tropical year and why calendars use the tropical one, then explain precession's role.

name: Mars Time
teaser: A sol — a Martian day — is 24 hours, 39 minutes and 35 seconds, about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day. It matters to every Mars mission: rover and orbiter teams live on Mars time, shifting their schedules by 40 minutes each day to match the red planet's rhythm. The extra time adds up: Mars has about 669 sols in a year, and a Mars year lasts 687 Earth days, nearly two Earth years. The word 'sol' was coined by astronomers to avoid confusion with Earth days. Mission controllers who work 'Mars time' famously end up living on a planet that never syncs with home.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how a sol on Mars differs from an Earth day and how mission teams adapt, then explain why rovers keep their own clocks.

name: The Longest Day
teaser: A day on Venus is longer than its year. Venus spins so slowly, backwards, that one rotation takes 243 Earth days — while it orbits the Sun in just 225 days. That means a solar day on Venus (sunrise to sunrise) lasts about 117 Earth days, and over a full Venusian year the Sun rises, sets and rises again less than twice. The slow, retrograde spin is one of the solar system's great oddities, likely the legacy of a massive ancient impact. If you lived on Venus, you'd see the Sun rise in the west, creep across the sky for two months, and set in the east — before a whole year had passed.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why a day on Venus outlasts its year, then explain how its slow backward spin makes that possible.

name: Atomic Clocks
teaser: Atomic clocks are the most accurate timekeepers ever built — devices that measure time by counting the vibrations of atoms, usually caesium-133, which oscillates 9.19 billion times per second. The best atomic clocks lose less than one second in 100 million years. They define the international standard second, keep GPS accurate, and underpin the world's financial networks. Today's optical lattice clocks are even more precise, probing time at levels where relativity itself must be corrected — a clock raised one centimetre runs measurably faster than one on the floor. Atomic clocks measure the fabric of time itself, and they're getting better every year.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how atomic clocks keep time with vibrating atoms and why they are so accurate, then explain their role in GPS and science.

name: Leap Seconds
teaser: Leap seconds are the tiny adjustments that keep our clocks in step with Earth's rotation - and they are causing a lot of debate. Atomic clocks are so accurate that they are essentially perfect, but Earth's spin is not: it slows by about 1.7 milliseconds per century, and it wobbles unpredictably. Since 1972, scientists have added 27 leap seconds to keep atomic time within 0.9 seconds of solar time. Leap seconds are a pain for computer systems, so in 2022 the world voted to phase them out by 2035, planning instead for a bigger leap minute every century or so. Our timekeeping is a constant negotiation between atomic perfection and the spinning planet beneath us.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why leap seconds are added and the debate over abolishing them, then explain what Earth's slowing spin has to do with it.

name: How Calendars Evolved
teaser: The calendar is one of humanity's oldest inventions — a way of counting the Sun's cycles. Early calendars were lunar, following the Moon's 29.5-day months, but they drifted out of sync with the seasons, so civilisations added corrections. The Egyptian solar calendar of 365 days, the Babylonian lunar-solar system, the Roman calendar with its reforms, and finally the Julian and Gregorian calendars each refined the fit. The week, the month, the year are all compromises between the Moon, the Sun and the needs of agriculture, religion and government. Behind every date on your phone lies thousands of years of trial, error and reform. Timekeeping is civilization's oldest software.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how calendars moved from lunar to solar and why months lost their lunar meaning, then explain the Gregorian reform.

name: The Gregorian Calendar
teaser: In October 1582, ten days vanished. Pope Gregory XIII's calendar reform corrected the drift of the Julian calendar — which had accumulated a 10-day error over 1,600 years — by decreeing that the day after October 4 would be October 15. The Gregorian calendar also refined leap years: century years are leap years only if divisible by 400, keeping the calendar aligned with the seasons for thousands of years. Catholic countries adopted it immediately; Protestant and Orthodox nations resisted for centuries — Britain didn't switch until 1752, when riots broke out over the 'lost' days. Today the Gregorian calendar is the world's standard, a triumph of astronomy turned into everyday life.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why the Gregorian calendar skipped days and how it fixed drift, then explain which countries adopted it late.

name: The Julian Calendar
teaser: The Julian calendar, introduced by Julius Caesar in 45 BC, was the first systematic solar calendar of the ancient world. Its innovation was simple but revolutionary: add one leap day every four years, keeping the calendar in step with the seasons. The calendar was designed with the help of Greek astronomers and replaced the wildly inaccurate Roman lunar calendar. It served Europe for over 1,600 years, but its slight over-correction - about 11 minutes a year - accumulated into a drift of 10 days by the 1500s. That drift prompted the Gregorian reform of 1582. Despite its flaw, the Julian calendar's basic structure of 365 days plus leap years survives unchanged today.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how the Julian calendar added leap years and why it drifted, then explain what Julius Caesar changed.

name: Lunar Calendars
teaser: Lunar calendars follow the Moon — twelve lunar months of 29 or 30 days, totaling about 354 days, some 11 days short of a solar year. The Islamic calendar is the purest example, drifting through the seasons on a 33-year cycle. Other traditions — the Hebrew, Chinese and Hindu calendars — are lunisolar: they add an extra month every few years to keep the lunar months aligned with the seasons. The Moon's phases were the first reliable timekeepers: the word 'month' comes from 'moon'. Even in the solar-based Gregorian world, the Moon still sets the rhythm of many festivals — Easter, Ramadan, the Chinese New Year.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how lunar calendars track the Moon and why they drift from the seasons, then explain how cultures add months to fix that.

name: The Birth of Time Zones
teaser: Time zones were born on the railways. In the 19th century, every town kept its own local solar time, and trains crossing between them created chaos — American railroads ran on dozens of different times. In 1883, the US railroads agreed on four standard time zones, and the 1884 International Meridian Conference in Washington set Greenwich as the prime meridian, dividing the world into 24 zones, mostly an hour apart. The idea spread globally over the following decades. Time zones made coordinated transport, communication and commerce possible — the world's clocks were synchronized for the first time in history. The railways did what kings and empires couldn't: they standardized time.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how railways forced the world to standardize time, then explain the role of Greenwich in the system.

name: The Speed of Light
teaser: Light speed — 299,792 km per second — is the universe's speed limit, the fastest anything can travel. In one second, light circles Earth seven and a half times; in eight minutes it crosses the 150 million km to the Sun; in 4.2 years it reaches the nearest star. Nothing with mass can reach light speed, and nothing can exceed it — this limit is built into the fabric of physics. The speed of light is also the conversion factor in Einstein's E=mc², showing how mass and energy are interchangeable. Every time you see the Moon, you see it a second and a half in the past. Light speed is the universe's constant heartbeat.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what the speed of light is and why nothing can beat it, then explain what it means for seeing the past.

name: Light-Minutes and Light-Hours
teaser: Astronomers measure distances in time: the light-minute, the distance light travels in a minute — about 18 million km. The Sun is 8.3 light-minutes away; the Moon, 1.3 light-seconds; Jupiter, between 33 and 53 light-minutes depending on its orbit. Communicating with Mars means waiting 4 to 24 minutes each way, and the delay shapes every mission. Using time as distance is natural — it's how fast light links us to everything — and it makes cosmic distances visceral: the Sun is eight minutes away, and we see it as it was eight minutes ago. Time and distance are two names for the same thing.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how far the Sun's light travels in minutes and hours, then explain why talking to Mars takes minutes.

name: Looking Back in Time
teaser: Every telescope is a time machine. Because light takes time to travel, looking farther out means looking further back — the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago, the nearest stars a few years ago, Andromeda 2.5 million years ago, and the James Webb Space Telescope's deepest images show galaxies as they were 13 billion years ago, not long after the Big Bang. When you look at the night sky, you're seeing a museum of the universe's past — each star and galaxy at a different moment in its history. The night sky is not a map of space; it's a map of time.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why looking far away means looking back in time, then explain what the most distant galaxies tell us about the young universe.

name: The Hubble Deep Field
teaser: The Hubble Deep Field is one of the most important images ever taken — a view of a tiny, seemingly empty patch of sky, no bigger than a grain of sand held at arm's length, that turned out to contain about 3,000 galaxies. Astronomers pointed Hubble at the patch for 10 days in 1995 and let the light accumulate; what emerged was a window into the early universe, with galaxies of every shape, size and colour, some so distant their light left when the universe was young. The Deep Field proved the universe is far richer than we imagined, and it's been repeated with even longer exposures, each one a deeper look back in time.

exploreAction.instruction: Discover how pointing Hubble at an empty patch revealed thousands of galaxies, then explain why the image changed astronomy.

name: Webb's Deep Fields
